us_fed.body: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
us_fed.ai_jurisdiction: The single most important AI door in the Senate. Owns the FTC (consumer protection, unfair/deceptive AI practices), NIST and the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), NTIA, NSF, NOAA, the FCC, interstate commerce generally, and commercial data privacy. Send here: general-purpose/frontier AI regulation, AI safety testing and evaluation mandates, federal preemption of state AI laws, AI transparency and disclosure rules, chatbots and minors, deepfakes/NCII, AI standards, commercial data privacy, autonomous vehicles, and AI in telecom. NOT here: copyright, liability/private rights of action, or DOJ (Judiciary); federal agency internal AI use (HSGAC); military AI (Armed Services); AI chip export controls (Banking).

us_fed.body: Subcommittee on Consumer Protection, Technology, and Data Privacy
us_fed.parent: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
us_fed.ai_jurisdiction: The FTC-facing consumer door. AI harms to individual consumers: deceptive AI claims, algorithmic pricing, AI chatbots and companion apps marketed to minors, dark patterns, commercial surveillance and data privacy as inputs to AI training, kids' online safety. This is where a parent, a consumer, or a state AG concern about a specific AI product lands. Not the venue for compute, export controls or model-level safety testing.

us_fed.body: Senate Committee on the Judiciary
us_fed.ai_jurisdiction: Rights, remedies and law enforcement. Send here: whether AI companies can be sued (duty of care, product liability, Section 230), AI and copyright/right of publicity, AI-generated CSAM and deepfakes as crimes, DOJ and FBI use of AI, antitrust in AI and cloud/compute markets, AI and immigration adjudication, and constitutional/civil-liberties questions. This is the liability door; Commerce is the regulation door.

us_fed.body: Subcommittee on Privacy, Technology, and the Law
us_fed.ai_jurisdiction: The named AI-oversight subcommittee of Senate Judiciary and the venue that produced the 2023-2024 'Oversight of AI' hearing series. Send here: AI and civil liberties, government and corporate surveillance, biometric and facial recognition, AI transparency and audit obligations framed as a legal duty, and whistleblower accounts from inside AI labs. Distinct from Commerce's consumer subcommittee: this one frames AI as a rights-and-rule-of-law problem rather than a marketplace problem.

us_fed.ai_jurisdiction: Criminal misuse of AI and, in the 119th Congress, the de facto venue for AI chatbot harms to children and vulnerable users. Also AI-enabled fraud and impersonation, AI-generated CSAM, and AI in terrorism and bioweapon uplift framed as a criminal matter.

us_fed.body: Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs
us_fed.ai_jurisdiction: How the federal government itself buys, builds and uses AI, plus DHS and CISA. Send here: federal AI procurement rules and contract terms, agency Chief AI Officers, AI risk management inside agencies, AI in federal benefits and enforcement decisions, government use of AI for surveillance or content moderation, GSA and OMB AI policy, federal AI workforce, and AI threats to critical infrastructure on the DHS side. NOT the place for rules on private-sector AI products.
us_fed.recent_activity: VERIFIED: S.3410 (Kim, D-NJ) to establish federal agency technology and AI talent teams — referred here. Peters is the committee's long-running AI-in-government legislator; his PREPARED for AI Act (risk-based federal AI procurement, Chief AI Officers, high-risk contract terms) was reported by this committee in the 118th Congress as S.4495 and remains the template for 119th Congress procurement work. Chairman Paul's AI emphasis is the opposite direction — restricting government use of AI for surveillance and speech moderation. UNVERIFIED: no specific 2026 full-committee AI hearing title confirmed; the committee's 2026 AI-adjacent activity is mostly bill referrals and oversight letters.

us_fed.body: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
us_fed.ai_jurisdiction: Export controls and financial-sector AI. This committee owns the Export Control Reform Act and the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security — so every question about AI chip export controls, location verification on advanced chips, and smuggling to China lands here, not in Foreign Relations. Also: AI in credit decisions, underwriting, insurance and fraud detection, algorithmic discrimination in lending, AI and financial stability, and CFIUS review of AI investments.

us_fed.body: Senate Committee on Armed Services
us_fed.ai_jurisdiction: Military AI and, through the NDAA, the one must-pass annual vehicle that reliably carries AI policy. us_fed.ai_jurisdiction: The House door for AI export controls and AI diplomacy. us_fed.body: Congressional Artificial Intelligence Caucus
us_fed.ai_jurisdiction: Not a jurisdictional body — no bills are referred here and it cannot hold official hearings or markups. Its function is member education and cross-committee coordination: briefings for members and staff, sign-on letters, and building bipartisan support before a bill reaches a committee of jurisdiction. Useful to a member of the public as a way to reach AI-attentive offices in bulk, and as a signal of who is engaged.
us_fed.recent_activity: VERIFIED: 16 Sep 2026 bipartisan letter to House leadership urging immediate action on AI guardrails, oversight, security and transparency, signed by Don Beyer, Jay Obernolte, Lori Trahan, Ted Lieu, Scott Franklin, Sara Jacobs, Gabe Amo, Valerie Foushee, Brian Fitzpatrick and Veronica Escobar (beyer.house.gov DocumentID 9218). 17 Sep 2026: Beyer publicly warned Congress 'may not receive another warning shot' on AI.

Caucus membership is for Members of Congress only; the public engages by contacting the co-chairs' offices or by asking their own representative to join.

Beyer and McCaul are listed as co-chairs; the 'chair'/'ranking' fields above are used to carry the two co-chairs, not a majority/minority relationship. Note the caucus historically ran from Rep. us_fed.ai_jurisdiction: Bipartisan member-education and coordination body founded in 2019. No referral jurisdiction. Its value is that its two co-chairs sit on the committees that matter — Heinrich is ranking member of Energy and Natural Resources and sits on Intelligence; Rounds chairs Armed Services' Cybersecurity subcommittee and sits on Banking — so the caucus functions as a bridge between the energy, defense and financial AI conversations.

Heinrich, Schumer, Rounds and Young were the four authors of the Senate's bipartisan AI policy roadmap. Heinrich, Young, Rounds and Booker reintroduced legislation to expand access to AI research (the CREATE AI / NAIRR line of work) in the 119th Congress. Rounds and Heinrich introduced legislation on AI for pandemic preparedness and response.

us_fed.body: House Bipartisan Task Force on Artificial Intelligence
us_fed.ai_jurisdiction: A leadership-appointed, time-limited body — not a committee — created by Speaker Mike Johnson and Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries in February 2024 and co-chaired by Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Ted Lieu (D-CA). It produced a comprehensive final report in December 2024 that remains the House's closest thing to a shared AI framework, organized by sector rather than by committee.
us_fed.recent_activity: VERIFIED: final report delivered December 2024 (118th Congress). NOT VERIFIED AS RECONSTITUTED IN THE 119th CONGRESS — no official announcement of a re-established task force was found as of 22 Sep 2026, and the 16 Sep 2026 bipartisan letter from Beyer, Obernolte, Lieu and seven others urging House leaders to act on AI is itself evidence that members are pressing leadership for renewed structured action. The live successor vehicle is the bipartisan 'Great American AI Act' discussion draft released 4 Jun 2026 by Trahan, Obernolte and Houchin.

For substantive AI policy input right now, the open channel is GAAIA@mail.house.gov, the public feedback address for the Great American AI Act draft.

us_fed.note: Co-chairs and report verified 2026-09-22 from obernolte.house.gov, lieu.house.gov and democraticleader.house.gov. Status as a currently constituted 119th Congress body is UNVERIFIED and appears to be dormant — this is a correction to any guide that lists it as active.

us_fed.body: Constituent route: chair and ranking member district and state offices
us_fed.ai_jurisdiction: Not a committee. This entry answers the brief's recurring question of whether a chair's own office beats the committee. Rule of thumb, verified against the contact structures above: for almost every committee in this list, a constituent should go to the member's own district or state office first, and a non-constituent should go to the committee or to an organization that has standing with it.
us_fed.recent_activity: Not applicable.
us_fed.public_route: Find your representative at https://www.house.gov/representatives/find-your-representative and your senators at https://www.senate.gov/senators/senators-contact.htm. Congressional offices systematically deprioritize mail from non-constituents; most Senate and House web forms require an in-state or in-district address and will reject others. Committee staff, by contrast, are policy staff who read substantive material regardless of its origin but have no casework obligation to anyone.
us_fed.statement_for_record: The highest-leverage move available to an ordinary member of the public is to ask their own representative or senator — if that member sits on a committee of jurisdiction — to submit their statement for the record, raise a question at a hearing, or sponsor an amendment. Members can insert material into a record; the public generally cannot do so directly outside the Appropriations public-witness windows.
us_fed.note: Guidance entry, included because the per-committee 'chair's own office vs committee' question has a consistent answer. Specific cases where the committee beats the member's office: House and Senate Appropriations during the spring public-witness window (open to all, formal record); House Judiciary, House Oversight, House Financial Services, Senate HSGAC/PSI and Senate Intelligence whistleblower intakes (open to all, for factual allegations); and GAAIA@mail.house.gov for the Great American AI Act draft (open to all).

us_state.body: Assembly Committee on Privacy and Consumer Protection
us_state.ai_jurisdiction: Primary Assembly committee of first referral for AI, algorithmic decision-making, chatbot, data-privacy and AI-transparency bills (e.g. SB 53, AB 1064, AB 1018, companion-chatbot bills). Also runs a joint hearing track with the Select Committee on Biotechnology and Medical Technology on AI in health.
us_state.key_legislation: SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act, Wiener) — signed 25 Sep 2025. 2026 follow-ons signed: SB 813 (independent verification organizations, signed 9 Sep 2026), AB 1405 (AI auditor registry, signed 9 Sep 2026), SB 1119 + SB 867 (companion chatbots / AI toys, signed 10 Sep 2026), AB 1709, AB 1856, AB 2246 (minors/design code, signed 10 Sep 2026), SB 1050 (synthetic performer disclosure, signed 16 Sep 2026). Pending on Governor's desk as of 22 Sep 2026: SB 1000, AB 2713, AB 1609, SB 1111, SB 947, AB 1883.
us_state.status: VERIFIED — SB 53 in force; CA Dept. of Technology begins annual threshold reviews in 2027. EO N-9-26 (18 Sep 2026) accelerates SB 813/AB 1405 implementation and directs work toward a frontier-model 'kill switch'. 2026 session closed; ~two dozen AI bills signed 9–16 Sep 2026.
us_state.public_testimony: YES — strongest and most underused route in the country. Any individual may register once and file a formal position letter (Support / Oppose / Amend) on any bill through the Legislature's Advocates portal; the letter is entered into the committee's official bill file and summarized in the committee analysis. Deadline convention for this committee: 12:00 noon on the Tuesday one week before the Tuesday hearing. Written testimony submitted this way is public comment and may be read into the record. In-person testimony at the hearing is open (two primary witnesses per side plus an open 'me-too' line); telephonic testimony has been discontinued.
us_state.agency_route: CA Attorney General (oag.ca.gov — AI legal advisories, Jan 2025; exclusive SB 53 civil enforcement); California Privacy Protection Agency for automated decision-making technology under the CCPA ADMT regs (https://cppa.ca.gov/regulations/ccpa_updates.html); California Civil Rights Department for FEHA automated-decision-system employment rules. Consumer complaints: https://oag.ca.gov/report
us_state.note: The position-letter portal is open to 'individuals' as a registration category, not just lobbyists — confirmed on the portal itself. This is the single highest-leverage public-participation channel in US state AI policy and is dominated by trade associations.

us_state.body: Senate Committee on Judiciary
us_state.ai_jurisdiction: Senate committee of first referral for frontier-AI safety, liability, digital replica, civil-rights and privacy AI bills. SB 53's Senate policy vehicle.

us_state.public_testimony: YES — position letters accepted from any member of the public via the Advocates portal, by email to sjud.fax@sen.ca.gov, by fax (916) 403-7394, or by mail (1021 O Street, Room 3240, Sacramento CA 95814). Deadline: 12:00 p.m. the Tuesday before the hearing unless otherwise stated. Committee staff explicitly warn they do not forward letters to individual members' offices, so copy members directly.

us_state.note: Committee letter-policy page and deadline verified on sjud.senate.ca.gov 22 Sep 2026. Member roster not enumerated on the landing page; use the site's Members tab.

us_state.ai_jurisdiction: Implementation and enforcement of SB 53, SB 813 and AB 1405; ADMT regulation; FEHA automated-decision rules.

us_state.body: Senate Standing Committee on Internet and Technology
us_state.ai_jurisdiction: Lead Senate committee for AI, frontier-model safety, algorithmic pricing, AI training-data transparency and companion-chatbot bills. Held a dedicated public hearing on AI in consequential/high-risk contexts on 15 Jan 2026.
us_state.key_legislation: RAISE Act, S6953B / A6453B (Gounardes / Bores) — signed 19 Dec 2025 (chapter amendments negotiated with Gov. Hochul). 2026 passed and awaiting Hochul action: A3411B (generative-AI inaccuracy notice, passed Senate 9 Mar 2026); A6578/S6955 (AI training-data transparency); A10379/S9051 (companion chatbots + 5-year AI children's-toy moratorium); A9349/S8623 (One Fair Price Act, surveillance pricing); A9581/S8706 (AI employment-impact reporting).

Two routes: (1) any New Yorker can register a formal position on any bill directly on its NYSenate.gov page using the 'Aye'/'Nay' buttons with a written comment — the position and comment are transmitted immediately to that person's own senator's office; this is free, open, and almost entirely unused by the public. (2) For a noticed committee public hearing, testimony is by hearing-specific reply form circulated with the hearing notice, filed in advance with the committee; written statements are accepted from anyone even without speaking.
us_state.agency_route: New York Attorney General — exclusive RAISE Act civil enforcement (complaints: https://ag.ny.gov/complaint-forms). Separate frontier-AI oversight office created inside the Department of Financial Services to assess large frontier developers, collect fees, issue regulations and publish annual reports (https://www.dfs.ny.gov).

us_state.body: Senate Committee on Business, Labor, & Technology
us_state.ai_jurisdiction: Senate committee of reference for AI, automated decision-making technology, consumer protection and technology bills. SB 26-189 was referred here.
us_state.key_legislation: SB 26-189 'Automated Decision-Making Technology' (Rodriguez, Coleman / Duran, Bacon) — repeals and replaces the Colorado AI Act (SB 24-205). Signed 14 May 2026, effective 1 Jan 2027. Predecessor history: SB 24-205 enacted 2024; SB 25B-004 (Aug 2025 special session) pushed its effective date to 30 Jun 2026; AG delayed enforcement Apr 2026; a federal court then restrained enforcement.
us_state.status: VERIFIED, WITH LITIGATION RISK — SB 26-189 drops SB 24-205's algorithmic-discrimination duty of care and risk-management program in favor of disclosure/transparency plus consumer rights over ADMT in consequential decisions. A federal district court ordered the AG not to initiate enforcement of SB 24-205 or replacement legislation for conduct occurring before 14 days after it rules on x.AI's preliminary-injunction motion, so the 1 Jan 2027 date is not secure.
us_state.public_testimony: YES — Colorado is one of the most open states. Any member of the public may testify in person OR remotely by video at a committee hearing, and may submit written testimony, after registering through the General Assembly's Public Testimony Registration system. Register in advance of the hearing (sign-ups typically open once the hearing is noticed and close shortly before it starts). Written testimony is accepted from anyone and is distributed to committee members.
us_state.agency_route: Colorado Attorney General — exclusive enforcement under the Colorado Consumer Protection Act; ADMT violations are deceptive trade practices. Complaints: https://coag.gov/file-complaint/
us_state.note: Vice Chair: Nick Hinrichsen. Members: Marc Catlin, Iman Jodeh, Larry Liston. See also https://content.leg.colorado.gov/agencies/senate/participation-legislative-hearings for the hearing-participation rules.

us_state.body: House Committee on Delivery of Government Efficiency
us_state.ai_jurisdiction: House committee that heard and reported TRAIGA (HB 149) in the 89th Legislature; jurisdiction over state technology, AI governance and government efficiency.
us_state.key_legislation: HB 149, Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act (TRAIGA), Capriglione — passed House 147-0, Senate 31-0; signed June 2025; IN FORCE since 1 January 2026. Companion 89R AI bills: SB 1964 (state-agency AI use), HB 2818 (AI Division inside DIR), SB 441 and HB 3133 (deepfakes), SB 2420 (App Store Accountability), SB 1188 (health records/AI), HB 3512 (state-employee AI training).
us_state.status: VERIFIED, IN FORCE — TRAIGA is intent-based, bars a private right of action, preempts local AI ordinances, gives the AG a 60-day cure period, creates a 7-member Texas Artificial Intelligence Council inside DIR and a 36-month AI regulatory sandbox administered by DIR.
us_state.public_testimony: YES, and unusually easy. Texas runs a dedicated online House Public Comment portal: any member of the public can submit a written comment for or against any bill set for a House committee hearing, from anywhere, without travelling to Austin. Comments are accepted from the time the hearing is posted until the committee closes the record (typically shortly after the hearing adjourns). In-person witness registration is done at Capitol kiosks or via the committee clerk. Note: 2026 is an interim year — the 90th Legislature convenes January 2027 — so the live route right now is interim-charge hearings.
us_state.agency_route: Texas Attorney General — sole TRAIGA enforcement authority; TRAIGA required the AG to stand up an online AI complaint mechanism. AI rights and complaint route: https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/consumer-protection/file-consumer-complaint/consumer-ai-rights ; portal: https://consumerprotection.texasattorneygeneral.gov/consumercomplaintportal/s/ . Civil penalties $10,000–$200,000.
us_state.note: Vice Chair: Salman Bhojani. Also relevant: Texas Artificial Intelligence Council (7 public members, within DIR) created by TRAIGA.

us_state.status: VERIFIED — TRAIGA in force since 1 Jan 2026; interim review under way through 2026 (committee took up AI and jobs in a hearing week of 21 Sep 2026).

Unlike the House there is no general online comment portal for Senate committees: register to testify with the committee clerk (Annika Vandayar, (512) 463-0365, Sam Houston Building Room 370) and submit written testimony to the clerk in advance, per the notice posted on Texas Legislature Online. Interim hearings are the most accessible moment because the record is open and the committee is actively taking input for 2027 bills.

us_state.note: Vice Chair: Phil King. Other 2026 interim AI charges sit with House State Affairs (data centers), House Public Health, House Public Education, House Judiciary & Civil Jurisprudence, and Senate Economic Development (AI workforce impact).

us_state.body: House Committee on Cybersecurity, Data Analytics, & IT (with its Artificial Intelligence Subcommittee, HCDA-HAIE)
us_state.ai_jurisdiction: Primary House committee for AI, data privacy, algorithmic systems and social-media bills. Has three standing subcommittees: Artificial Intelligence (HAIE), Data Privacy and Analytics (HDPA), and Social Media and Content Moderation (HSMC).
us_state.key_legislation: SB 315, Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act — Senate sponsor Sen. Mary Edly-Allen (D-Grayslake), House sponsor Rep. Daniel Didech (D-Buffalo Grove). Passed Senate 52-5 and House 110-0; signed by Gov. Pritzker 6 July 2026; effective 1 January 2027 (some analyses cite full compliance obligations phasing to 2028). Also in force: HB 3773 (AI in employment decisions under the Illinois Human Rights Act, effective 1 Jan 2026); the AI Video Interview Act; and the WOPR Act restricting AI therapy.
us_state.status: VERIFIED for the legislation; UNVERIFIED for the chair. SB 315 is the first US state law to require independent third-party safety audits of frontier developers (models from developers with >$500M annual revenue), publication of safety frameworks, catastrophic-risk reporting, and 72-hour (24-hour for imminent risk) incident reporting. Enforced by the Illinois Attorney General with penalties up to $1M first violation / $3M subsequent.
us_state.public_testimony: YES — Illinois has the single most frictionless public-position system of any state: the electronic WITNESS SLIP. Any person may file a slip on any bill before any committee hearing, recording their name, whether they represent themselves or an organization, and their position (Proponent / Opponent / No Position), with an option to request to testify orally or submit a record of appearance only. No lobbyist registration, no fee. Slips are counted and displayed publicly and legislators visibly react to the tallies. Deadline convention: file at least one hour before the hearing (ideally the day before); the Senate accepts and allows edits until the end of the hearing day, the House until the hearing concludes. A separate slip is required for each committee hearing and for each amendment.
us_state.agency_route: Illinois Attorney General — enforcement of the AI Safety Measures Act; consumer fraud complaints at https://www.illinoisattorneygeneral.gov/file-a-complaint/consumer/ . For AI employment discrimination under HB 3773: Illinois Department of Human Rights (dhr.illinois.gov).
us_state.note: CHAIR UNVERIFIED — the ILGA site blocked automated retrieval of the committee detail page and no 2025–2026 source names the chair. Prior chairs (Jaime Andrade 2017, Lamont Robinson 2023) have both left the role. Verify by phone with the House Clerk or at ilga.gov/House/Committees. Committee composition for 2025–2026 is 8 Democrats / 4 Republicans. Witness slips are filed from the specific hearing page, e.g. https://ilga.gov/House/hearings — the linked PDF is the official ILGA tutorial.

us_state.ai_jurisdiction: Explicitly holds artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, broadband and telecommunications jurisdiction. All three major 2026 AI bills were heard here on 15 Jan 2026.
us_state.key_legislation: HB 2225 (AI companion chatbots, prime sponsor Rep. Lisa Callan, by request of Gov. Ferguson) — House 69-28, Senate 43-5, concurrence 74-21, SIGNED 24 March 2026 as Chapter 168, Laws of 2026, effective 1 January 2027; companion SB 5984. us_state.public_testimony: YES — Washington's Committee Sign-In (CSI) system is the best-designed remote testimony portal in the country and is wide open. For any scheduled hearing, any member of the public can (a) sign in PRO / CON / OTHER on a bill in under a minute with no account and no travel — these positions are tallied and reported to the committee; (b) submit written testimony that becomes part of the legislative record; or (c) register to testify remotely by video or in person. Deadline convention: written testimony and position sign-in generally close one hour before the hearing; remote-testimony registration typically closes 24 hours before. Meetings are hybrid by default.
us_state.agency_route: Washington Attorney General — Consumer Protection Division (https://www.atg.wa.gov/file-complaint); the AG's Office also hosts the statutory Washington State AI Task Force.

Deadline convention: written testimony must be submitted before the start of the hearing (committees typically post a cut-off of 24 hours prior for guaranteed distribution); speaker sign-up for major hearings is by lottery opening roughly 24 hours before. All testimony — written and spoken — is permanent public record, posted on the CGA website and indexed by search engines, including your name, address, phone and email.

us_state.key_legislation: December 2025 Executive Order establishing an AI Litigation Task Force to challenge state AI laws deemed not 'minimally burdensome', and directing Commerce to explore withholding BEAD broadband funding from states enacting 'onerous' AI laws. The order signaled carve-outs for child safety and AI compute/data-center infrastructure.
us_state.status: VERIFIED — as of 1 July 2026 states had still enacted 109 AI laws and 28 data-center laws in 2026, versus 121 and 27 at the same point in 2025. uk_eu.body: European Parliament — the rapporteur and shadow rapporteur system (the highest-leverage seats in EU legislating)
uk_eu.ai_jurisdiction: Applies to every AI legislative file. WHAT A RAPPORTEUR IS: when the Commission sends a legislative proposal to Parliament, one committee is designated lead. Within that committee the political groups bid for the file using an auction system based on group size, and the winning group appoints ONE MEP as rapporteur. That single MEP drafts Parliament's report — the consolidated set of amendments that becomes Parliament's official position — decides which of the thousands of tabled amendments are folded into compromise texts, chairs the technical meetings, and then personally leads Parliament's delegation in the closed trilogue negotiations with the Council and Commission where the final law is actually written. WHAT A SHADOW RAPPORTEUR IS: every other political group appoints one shadow to follow the same file. Shadows negotiate the compromise amendments with the rapporteur; a compromise that the EPP, S&D and Renew shadows sign will pass, and one they refuse will not. The rapporteur plus roughly six shadows — under ten people — effectively write EU law on a given file. This is why the rapporteur seat is worth more than a committee chair: the chair runs the meeting, the rapporteur writes the text.

uk_eu.public_route: HOW AN OUTSIDER ACTUALLY REACHES A RAPPORTEUR: (1) Identify the file and its holders in the Legislative Observatory (oeil.europarl.europa.eu) or the Legislative Train (europarl.europa.eu/legislative-train) — both list the procedure number, lead committee and rapporteur. (2) Go to that MEP's page at europarl.europa.eu/meps/en/<id> which publishes their Brussels and Strasbourg office email and phone. (3) Write to the rapporteur AND every shadow at once — reaching only the rapporteur means your point dies if their group disagrees with it. (4) Time it to the draft-report and amendment-tabling window, which is the only period at which text can still change; after a trilogue deal nothing moves. (5) Say what you want in amendment form: name the article, give replacement wording, give one paragraph of justification. Rapporteurs' assistants triage hundreds of submissions and the ones that arrive as usable text get used. (6) An MEP office will normally meet a credible outside party; ask for a 20-minute meeting with the policy adviser, not the MEP. If you are paid to do this you must register on the EU Transparency Register first.
uk_eu.format_rules: No word limit, no portal, no deadline other than the committee's amendment-tabling deadline (published on the file page). Correspondence is not published. If you are an interest representative, entry in the EU Transparency Register is a precondition of meeting MEPs holding rapporteur roles, and such meetings must be declared.

uk_eu.body: European Parliament — Committee on Petitions (PETI)
uk_eu.ai_jurisdiction: PETI has no AI portfolio of its own, but it is the ONLY formal channel through which a private individual can compel the European Parliament to consider a matter. An admissible AI petition — for example on AI Act non-enforcement in a Member State, biometric surveillance, or algorithmic discrimination — is put to the committee, can trigger questions to the Commission, a committee debate, a fact-finding visit, or a referral to LIBE or IMCO.

chair.name: Bogdan Rzońca (ECR, Poland, Prawo i Sprawiedliwość)
chair.role: Chair

uk_eu.key_people: Vice-Chairs: Dolors Montserrat (EPP, ES); Fredis Beleris (EPP, GR); Nils Ušakovs (S&D, LV); Cristina Guarda (Greens/EFA, IT). The committee has 35 members.
uk_eu.current_business: Ordinary petition sittings roughly monthly; agendas published as PETI_OJ documents on europarl.europa.eu/doceo.
uk_eu.public_route: WHO MAY PETITION: 'Any citizen of the European Union, or resident in a Member State', individually or collectively, and 'any company, organisation or association with its headquarters in the European Union'. SUBJECT MATTER: the petition must concern a matter 'which comes within the European Union's fields of activity and which affects them directly' — this is the admissibility test and the most common reason petitions are rejected. It may be a complaint, a request, or an observation on the application of EU law, or an appeal for Parliament to take a position. PROCESS: file through the Petitions Web Portal in any of the 24 official EU languages; the secretariat assesses admissibility; admissible petitions go to the committee, which may ask the Commission for a preliminary investigation, put the petition on a meeting agenda, invite the petitioner to speak, refer it to another committee for opinion, or close it with a reasoned reply. THRESHOLD: there is NO signature threshold — one person suffices. (Do not confuse this with the European Citizens' Initiative, which does require one million signatures across at least seven Member States; that is a separate instrument aimed at the Commission, not Parliament.)
uk_eu.format_rules: No word limit. Available in all 24 official EU languages. Petitions and the committee's handling of them are published on the petitions portal unless the petitioner requests confidentiality. You may support an existing petition rather than filing a new one.
uk_eu.note: VERIFIED 2026-09-22: chair from the official PETI member list PDF; eligibility and subject-matter wording quoted from the European Parliament's own 'Be heard — petitions' page at europarl.europa.eu/at-your-service/en/be-heard/petitions.

uk_eu.body: European Commission — Executive Vice-President for Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy
uk_eu.ai_jurisdiction: The Commissioner-level holder of the digital and AI portfolio: owns the AI Act's implementation through DG CNECT and the AI Office, the Digital Omnibus simplification agenda, the Cloud and AI Development Act, the Apply AI strategy, and AI gigafactory/compute policy. The Commission has the exclusive right of legislative initiative, so this is where AI files begin.

chair.name: Henna Virkkunen
chair.role: Executive Vice-President of the European Commission for Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy

uk_eu.key_people: Operational work sits with DG CNECT and the European AI Office within it.
uk_eu.current_business: AI Act implementation following the Digital Omnibus on AI (adopted 16 June 2026, delaying high-risk system standards and banning 'nudifier' applications); Cloud and AI Development Act proposed 3 June 2026.
uk_eu.public_route: Respond to open consultations on the 'Have your say' portal; write to the Cabinet; or use the AI Act Service Desk for regulatory questions. Commission consultations are open to anyone worldwide, not only EU residents.
uk_eu.format_rules: Consultation responses are normally published on the initiative's feedback page together with the respondent's name and country, and organisations must give their EU Transparency Register number. You can ask for anonymity. Feedback periods for a 'call for evidence' are typically 4 weeks; full public consultations run 12 weeks.
uk_eu.note: VERIFIED 2026-09-22 from the European Commission's College of Commissioners page.

uk_eu.body: European Commission — European AI Office (within DG CNECT)
uk_eu.ai_jurisdiction: The EU's central AI regulator and the enforcement body for the AI Act's rules on general-purpose AI models. Three functions: (1) AI Act implementation and enforcement, including 'developing tools, methodologies and benchmarks for evaluating capabilities' of GPAI models and investigating possible violations; (2) fostering trustworthy AI, including sandboxes and real-world testing; (3) international AI governance coordination. Over 125 staff across 6 units plus 2 adviser posts.

chair.role: Head of the AI Office — not named on the official AI Office page as at this check

uk_eu.key_people: Governance bodies that carry outside voices into the AI Office: the AI Board (Member State representatives); the Scientific Panel of independent experts; the Advisory Forum, which is explicitly designed for balanced stakeholder representation including civil society; the AI Pact for business; and the Apply AI Alliance.
uk_eu.current_business: GPAI model oversight, AI Act guidelines (including on high-risk classification and transparency obligations), the Code of Practice process, and implementation of the changes made by the Digital Omnibus on AI.
uk_eu.public_route: Four concrete routes: (1) general enquiries to CNECT-AIOFFICE@ec.europa.eu; (2) the AI Act Service Desk for regulatory questions; (3) the Expression of Interest form for collaboration, which is how outside experts get onto drafting and consultation groups; (4) respond to AI Office consultations on draft guidelines, which are announced on the Shaping Europe's Digital Future consultations page. The Advisory Forum is the formal civil-society seat.
uk_eu.format_rules: Consultations on draft AI Act guidelines are typically 4–8 weeks and run through structured online questionnaires. Responses may be published. Recent examples VERIFIED on the consultations page: 'Targeted consultation on the draft guidelines for the classification of high-risk artificial intelligence systems' (19 May – 23 July 2026); 'Consultation on the draft guidelines on transparency obligations under the AI Act' (8 May – 3 June 2026); 'European Commission survey: AI in healthcare and pharmaceuticals' (2 – 26 June 2026). All three have closed; the page is the live index to whatever is open now.
uk_eu.note: VERIFIED 2026-09-22 from the Commission's own AI Office page and consultations index. The head of the AI Office is NOT named on the official page and I am not guessing at it. NOTE: the three AI consultations I could verify have all closed — as at 22 Sep 2026 I found no open AI consultation, but the index page is dynamic and should be checked directly.

uk_eu.body: European Commission — 'Have your say' consultation portal
uk_eu.ai_jurisdiction: The single entry point for public input to every EU legislative initiative before it is proposed, including all AI initiatives. Each initiative passes through a 'call for evidence' stage and often a full public consultation, both open to comment.

chair.role: Not applicable — administered by the Commission's Secretariat-General

uk_eu.current_business: AI-related initiatives that have used the portal include 'Artificial intelligence strategy for the cultural and creative sectors' (initiative 18592) and the Apply AI Strategy consultation. Open/closed status changes constantly — the portal's own search is the only reliable source.
uk_eu.public_route: Anyone in the world may register an EU Login account and submit feedback on any published initiative. This is the least gatekept formal channel in the entire EU system: no residency, nationality, or organisational requirement.
uk_eu.format_rules: Feedback is limited to 4,000 characters plus an attachment (normally one document up to 1MB). Calls for evidence typically run 4 weeks; full public consultations 12 weeks. Feedback is PUBLISHED on the initiative's feedback page with your name, your organisation and your country; organisations must supply an EU Transparency Register number. Anonymity can be requested.
uk_eu.note: PARTIALLY VERIFIED 2026-09-22. The portal URL and the existence of AI initiatives on it are verified from Commission pages. The 4,000-character limit and 4-week/12-week convention are standard Better Regulation practice but I could NOT re-verify them on 22 Sep 2026 because the portal page returned only metadata to my fetcher — treat those two figures as UNVERIFIED and check the portal before relying on them.

uk_eu.body: Members of the European Parliament — direct correspondence
uk_eu.ai_jurisdiction: Every MEP can table amendments, ask written questions of the Commission (which must be answered and are published), sign motions, and speak in committee. On AI, a single MEP's written question can force the Commission to state a position on the record.

chair.role: 720 MEPs

uk_eu.key_people: For AI specifically: Michael McNamara (Renew, IE), Brando Benifei (S&D, IT), Arba Kokalari (EPP, SE), Reinier van Lanschot (Greens/EFA, NL), plus the four committee chairs listed separately.
uk_eu.public_route: Find MEPs at the MEP directory, which searches by member name and by country. Each MEP's individual page publishes their Brussels and Strasbourg office addresses, phone numbers and email. CRUCIAL POINT FOR OUTSIDERS: MEPs are elected from multi-member constituencies (often the whole country) under proportional representation, so you have many MEPs, not one. There is no constituency-service convention equivalent to the UK's — MEPs routinely accept and act on correspondence from people who are not their voters, including from other Member States and from outside the EU, and they are not obliged to refuse it. In practice the group and the committee portfolio matter far more than geography: write to the MEP who holds the AI file, whatever country they represent. Parliament also runs a general citizens' enquiry service ('Ask EP') for questions about the EU and Parliament's work.
uk_eu.format_rules: No limits. Correspondence is not published. Replies are at the MEP's discretion; a specific, short, evidenced request to a policy adviser gets a far higher response rate than a mass-campaign email.
uk_eu.note: VERIFIED 2026-09-22: the MEP directory and the 'Write to us' / Ask EP form are both live official European Parliament pages. The statement that MEPs generally accept non-constituent correspondence reflects the structure of EU elections (no single-member constituencies) rather than a written rule I could cite.

uk_eu.body: House of Commons Standing Committee on Industry and Technology (INDU)
uk_eu.ai_jurisdiction: The lead Commons committee for AI. Industry, science, technology, telecommunications, competition and innovation policy. It was the committee that studied Bill C-27 (which contained the Artificial Intelligence and Data Act) clause by clause, and it is now running a dedicated AI study.

chair.name: Ben Carr, MP (Liberal, Winnipeg South Centre, Manitoba)
chair.role: Chair

uk_eu.key_people: Vice-Chairs: Raquel Dancho (Conservative, Kildonan—St. Paul) and Gabriel Ste-Marie (Bloc Québécois, Joliette—Manawan). Members: Parm Bains, Karim Bardeesy, Doly Begum, Adam Chambers (CPC), Harb Gill (CPC), Jason Groleau (CPC), Leslyn Lewis (CPC), Michael Ma, Bienvenu-Olivier Ntumba, Dominique O'Rourke.
uk_eu.current_business: Four active studies as at 22 Sep 2026, including 'Opportunities, Risks, and Regulation of AI in Canada's Strategic Industries'. The others: Financial Fraud and Scams in Canada; Federal Government's Electric Vehicle Policies; U.S. Tariffs and the Canadian Metallurgical Sector.
uk_eu.public_route: Submit a brief. Canada's brief system is the most open of the five jurisdictions here: 'Any individual or organization may submit a brief to a committee of the House of Commons, even if they are not given the opportunity to appear.' You do not need an invitation and you do not need to be Canadian. Send it to the committee clerk by email or through the online form; contact details are on the committee page.
uk_eu.format_rules: EXACT RULES: a brief should not exceed 10 pages. If longer, you must include a summary of no more than 500 words, which the committee may translate and distribute INSTEAD of the full document — so the 500-word summary is the part that actually gets read. May be submitted in either official language; the clerk coordinates translation, so submit early. Identify the author/organisation clearly on the cover; put your personal contact details in the covering email, NOT on the cover page. Support claims with concise factual information; put specific, summarised recommendations at the end; cite all quoted material in footnotes or a bibliography; visuals in black and white and preferably bilingual. Briefs become part of the committee's public archives, may be posted on the committee website, and submitters are listed in committee reports.
uk_eu.note: VERIFIED 2026-09-22 from the INDU committee page and the official 'Guide for submitting briefs to House of Commons Committees' at ourcommons.ca/procedure/guides/brief-e.html.

uk_eu.body: House of Commons Standing Committee on Access to Information, Privacy and Ethics (ETHI)
uk_eu.ai_jurisdiction: Privacy, data protection and ethics oversight — the committee that handles algorithmic and automated decision-making from a rights and privacy angle, facial recognition, and government use of AI tools. The natural home for AI-and-privacy work now that AIDA is dead and the privacy half of Bill C-27 has been reintroduced separately.

chair.role: Chair

uk_eu.format_rules: Max 10 pages, or a 500-word summary if longer; either official language; published on the committee website and listed in reports.
uk_eu.note: VERIFIED 2026-09-22 from the ETHI committee page. Note the chair is an opposition (Conservative) MP — ETHI is one of the committees chaired by the Official Opposition under Canadian practice.

uk_eu.body: House of Commons of Canada — committee brief submission system (the public route)
uk_eu.ai_jurisdiction: The mechanism, not a body. Every Commons standing, special and legislative committee accepts briefs from the public on any study it is conducting.

chair.role: Administered by each committee's clerk

uk_eu.public_route: Go to the committee's page, find the active study, and send a brief to the clerk by email or the online form. No invitation is needed. This is genuinely underused: most Canadian committee studies receive a small number of briefs, so a well-made one is disproportionately likely to be quoted in the report. You may also ask to appear as a witness — the request is made to the clerk in the same email.
uk_eu.format_rules: Maximum 10 pages. Longer briefs require a summary of no more than 500 words, and the committee may translate and circulate only that summary. English or French; the clerk arranges translation, and members will not receive the brief until it exists in both languages — so submit well before the study's hearings end. Author identified on the cover, personal contact details in the email only. Briefs become public archives, may be published online, and authors are listed in the committee's report.
uk_eu.note: VERIFIED 2026-09-22 against the official procedural guide at ourcommons.ca/procedure/guides/brief-e.html.

uk_eu.body: Government of Canada — Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation
uk_eu.ai_jurisdiction: Canada's dedicated AI portfolio. Owns the national AI strategy and the federal government's response to the collapse of AI legislation.

chair.name: The Hon. Evan Solomon
chair.role: Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation (also Minister responsible for the Federal Economic Development Agency for Southern Ontario)

uk_eu.current_business: AIDA'S STATUS AND WHAT REPLACED IT: the Artificial Intelligence and Data Act was Part 3 of Bill C-27 (Digital Charter Implementation Act, 2022). It died on the Order Paper when Parliament was prorogued in January 2025 and was never reintroduced. Canada therefore has NO general AI statute as at September 2026. What replaced it is not a law but a strategy plus targeted bills: 'AI for All', Canada's national AI strategy, launched by Prime Minister Mark Carney on 4 June 2026, built on three pillars (trust, opportunity, sovereignty), targeting a rise in AI adoption from 12% to 60% by 2034 and 250,000 new AI-related jobs over five years. Alongside it: the Protecting Victims Act (introduced December 2025) to prohibit distribution of non-consensual sexual deepfakes, and new legislation tabled in June 2026 on children's data and privacy. Commitments to modernise digital frameworks cover deepfakes and surveillance pricing.
uk_eu.public_route: Write to the minister; respond to Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada consultations; or, more effectively, put the point into an INDU brief where it enters the parliamentary record.
uk_eu.format_rules: Ministerial correspondence is not published and has no set format.
uk_eu.note: VERIFIED 2026-09-22 from the Prime Minister of Canada's official news release of 4 June 2026 launching AI for All, which names Evan Solomon in that portfolio. AIDA's death by prorogation is well established; I did not find any successor AI bill, and I am explicitly NOT claiming one exists.

uk_eu.body: Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence
uk_eu.ai_jurisdiction: Australia's principal current AI inquiry body, appointed by resolution of BOTH the House of Representatives and the Senate on 20 August 2026. Its terms of reference are unusually broad and are the best single statement of Australian AI policy scope: AI's contribution to resilience, productivity, competitiveness and living standards; spreading benefits to suburbs and regions; AI and robotics in research, new industries and exports (agriculture, resources, health and medical research, advanced manufacturing, financial services, defence industry); rate and barriers to adoption by SMEs and family businesses; sovereign AI capability and its commercialisation, R&D, investment and talent; data sovereignty and narrow domain-specific models trained on Australian data; workforce and skills implications including job creation and displacement and job quality and security; adoption of AI by Commonwealth departments and agencies and the transparency and accountability measures applying to it; THE ADEQUACY OF AUSTRALIA'S EXISTING LAWS AND REGULATORY FRAMEWORKS AS THEY APPLY TO AI AND WHETHER THERE ARE GAPS WARRANTING REFORM; AI's interaction with intellectual property and copyright law including use of Australian creative, cultural and media content in training; risks and harms including fraud and scams, deepfakes and risks to children and vulnerable Australians; national security and cyber security opportunities and foreign interference risks including supply chains and critical infrastructure; and the implications of emerging AI capability for national security and strategic resilience, including the ability of regulators, THE AUSTRALIAN AI SAFETY INSTITUTE and the intelligence and security community to identify and respond to emerging risks.

chair.role: Chair

Late submissions are sometimes accepted at the secretariat's discretion — ask. Secretariat: Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence, PO Box 6100, Parliament House, Canberra ACT 2600; phone +61 2 6277 3863; ai.joint@aph.gov.au.

It also draws attention to the advice that 'if you are making a submission to a committee, you are responsible for the quality and accuracy of the content of that submission, including where AI tools have been used' — an explicit warning against AI-generated submissions. Submissions are published only after the committee accepts and authorises them; you may not disclose your own submission until then.

uk_eu.body: Parliament of Australia — public submission system (the public route)
uk_eu.ai_jurisdiction: The mechanism by which any person reaches any Australian parliamentary committee, including all the AI inquiries above.

chair.role: Administered by each committee secretariat

uk_eu.current_business: Live index of every Senate, House and Joint inquiry currently accepting submissions is maintained at the Submissions_Open pages.
uk_eu.public_route: EXACT PROCESS, from the Parliament's own guidance: 'Any interested individual or organisation can make a submission to a parliamentary committee. Several people or organisations can make a joint submission. Organisations and people from other countries can make submissions to an inquiry' — though parliamentary privilege 'cannot be enforced outside Australia'. Lodge online via the link on the inquiry home page after creating a free My Parliament account (name and valid email only); or send directly by email or post to the committee secretariat. You can upload multiple documents, e.g. a covering letter, a public submission and a confidential attachment. An acknowledgement is emailed on receipt. If you cannot meet the deadline, a short extension is often possible — contact the secretariat.
uk_eu.format_rules: No word limit in general (individual committees may ask for brevity — the Joint Select Committee on AI asked for 5–6 pages). Upload as Word, PDF or plain text. PROCESS AND PUBLICATION: the secretariat assesses the submission, then the COMMITTEE decides whether to accept it and authorise publication, and may publish only part of it. Once authorised, personal details are removed and it is placed on the website and forms part of the formal record. YOUR OBLIGATIONS: 'After a submission is received by a committee, you cannot publish or disclose it to any other person unless or until the committee has authorised its publication' — this is a real constraint, breach of which can be a contempt. You cannot withdraw or alter a submission without the committee's permission. Confidential submissions may not be shared with anyone. If you submit by an organisation, the organisation is published as the author, not an individual.
uk_eu.note: VERIFIED 2026-09-22 by direct fetch of aph.gov.au 'Making a submission to a committee inquiry'. All quoted text is from that page.

uk_eu.ai_jurisdiction: The Commonwealth department that owns AI policy: the safe and responsible AI consultation and the Government's interim response, the proposed mandatory guardrails for high-risk AI, the AI Adopt Program, and coordination of Australia's international AI engagement including GPAI. The National Artificial Intelligence Centre, hosted at CSIRO's Data61, 'coordinates Australia's AI expertise and capabilities to address barriers for small and medium enterprises'. uk_eu.body: Economic Development, Science and Innovation Committee (54th Parliament)
uk_eu.ai_jurisdiction: The New Zealand select committee whose subject area covers AI. Its stated remit: 'business development, tourism, Crown minerals, commerce, consumer protection and trading standards, research, science, innovation, intellectual property, broadcasting, communications, and information technology.' AI sits inside 'research, science, innovation' and 'information technology', and AI-and-copyright inside 'intellectual property'. This is New Zealand's default destination for an AI bill, petition or briefing.

chair.name: Dr Parmjeet Parmar, MP (ACT Party, List)
chair.role: Chairperson

uk_eu.key_people: 8 members in total; the full list is on the committee's members page.

uk_eu.public_route: Two routes. (1) Make a submission when the committee calls for them on a bill or inquiry — the live list of items open for submissions is on the select committees home page. (2) Petition the House: a petition can be lodged by any person, goes to the Petitions Committee, and is then routinely referred to the relevant subject committee such as this one. You may ask to make an oral submission in person, by phone or by video conference; remote appearance is explicitly offered to people outside Wellington and to disabled submitters. If the meeting is livestreamed your submission will appear publicly. Advisers read and analyse all submissions and summarise them for the committee in a departmental report, which is also published.

uk_eu.body: Petitions Committee (54th Parliament)
uk_eu.ai_jurisdiction: No AI subject matter of its own, but it is the door through which a member of the public — including a single individual — puts a new issue such as AI regulation onto Parliament's agenda when no inquiry is open. It can refer a petition to a subject committee such as Economic Development, Science and Innovation, refer it to a Minister for response, or nominate it for debate in the House.

chair.name: Greg O'Connor, MP (Labour Party, Ōhāriu)
chair.role: Chairperson

uk_eu.current_business: A rolling caseload — 318 petitions listed in the committee's business index as at 22 September 2026, with new petitions presented that same day.
uk_eu.public_route: Anyone may start a petition to the House of Representatives — there is no signature threshold for presenting one, and petitions with a single signature are accepted. uk_eu.ai_jurisdiction: The mechanism for reaching any New Zealand select committee, including on any future AI bill.

A team of advisers reads and analyses all submissions and reports the results to the committee in a departmental report; both that report and the committee's report to the House are published.

uk_eu.body: Joint Committee on Artificial Intelligence (Houses of the Oireachtas)
uk_eu.ai_jurisdiction: A DEDICATED standing AI committee — the only one of its kind among the jurisdictions in this survey. Its stated remit, quoted from the Oireachtas: it 'was established to examine and make recommendations on Ireland's approach to the development, deployment, regulation, and ethical considerations of artificial intelligence (AI), and on the means of ensuring that the approach supports economic growth, innovation, public trust, and societal benefit while safeguarding rights and mitigating risks.' Established 12 May 2025, drawn from the 34th Dáil and 27th Seanad.
