orgs.name: ControlAI
orgs.the_ask: Governments should pass binding law prohibiting the development of superintelligent AI, and coordinate internationally to enforce that prohibition.
orgs.what_they_do: Lawmaker briefings and a model bill; a mass newsletter (claims 148,000+ subscribers); media work; a constituent-to-legislator contact tool; organised a letter from 70+ cross-party UK MPs and Peers to the Prime Minister asking the government to evaluate its bill.
orgs.newcomer_action: Use the contact tool at act.controlai.org to email or write to your lawmakers asking them to back a ban on superintelligence development; subscribe to the weekly newsletter; ask to join a local action group.
orgs.tips: No public tip line; offers briefings to lawmakers and journalists via hello@controlai.com
orgs.geography: UK, US, Canada, Germany. UK not-for-profit company limited by guarantee; US 501(c)(4).
orgs.scale: Roughly 20+ staff and advisors listed on its About page. Well-resourced relative to most groups here.
orgs.spending: Not disclosed. Homepage states it is 'only accepting substantial donations, except in special cases' — i.e. it is not running a small-donor programme.
orgs.caution: Its own action page says '205+ lawmakers support our campaign'; its homepage breaks that down as 160+ UK and 35+ Canadian lawmakers, plus 400+ lawmakers briefed across four countries. 'Support' means signing a campaign statement, not voting for a bill — no such bill has passed. The ask is a prohibition, not regulation; joining means endorsing a ban. Small donors are effectively not wanted.

orgs.name: PauseAI (PauseAI Global)
orgs.the_ask: Stop the development of the most powerful general AI systems, internationally, until we know how to make them safe.
orgs.what_they_do: Federation of local chapters coordinated by a global entity; petitions, protests, an email-your-representative builder, lobbying guides, 'microcommits' (weekly bite-sized actions), microgrants and volunteer stipends.
orgs.newcomer_action: Sign the PauseAI statement and the 'Say No To Superintelligent AI' petition (5 minutes), join the Discord, then use the email builder to write to your representative.
orgs.tips: No formal tip line; contact form and Discord
orgs.geography: International. Legally Stichting PauseAI (KvK 92951031), Netherlands. Local communities in many countries.
orgs.scale: Small paid core (CEO, Organizing Director, Communications Director; chapter directors paid by PauseAI Global) plus a large volunteer base. Budget not published.
orgs.spending: Not disclosed. Accepts donations at pauseai.info/donate.
orgs.caution: The ask is a halt to frontier development, not tighter rules. Protest-based but explicitly lawful — distinct from StopAI. Chapters vary a lot in activity; check your local one is alive before committing.

orgs.name: PauseAI US
orgs.the_ask: The United States should lead an international treaty to pause frontier AI development, and should pass domestic bills including a 'kill switch' and an AI Risk Evaluation Act.
orgs.what_they_do: Grassroots lobbying (trains volunteers then arranges constituent meetings with members of Congress), petitions, local groups, protests outside OpenAI and Anthropic offices, film screenings and educational events.
orgs.newcomer_action: Sign the treaty petition, send the pre-written emails on the AI Risk Evaluation Act and Kill Switch Act, then apply via the lobbying form to be trained and matched to a meeting with your representative.
orgs.scale: Small 501(c)(3) (EIN 99-0899650, San Francisco). Median donation about $100 — a genuinely small-donor, volunteer-driven operation.
orgs.caution: Legally and financially separate from PauseAI Global (Dutch foundation) and PauseAI UK — a US 501(c)(3) with its own EIN and board. Shares the movement's name and broad ask but sets its own US legislative priorities. The ask is a development pause, which most US lawmakers do not currently support; expect to be advocating a minority position.

orgs.name: PauseAI UK
orgs.the_ask: The UK should act to avert risks from superhuman AI, including binding frontier AI legislation.
orgs.what_they_do: Community-led organising through six local chapters (London, Glasgow, Oxford, Leicester, Manchester, West of England); meetups, book launches, public events; submissions to parliamentary inquiries including the Future of the Workforce inquiry; publishes playbooks for starting new local groups.
orgs.newcomer_action: Fill in the onboarding form, join the WhatsApp community, and turn up to the next event on its Luma calendar — or use the playbook to start a group in your city.
orgs.scale: Very small: a UK Director (Joseph Miller) and Deputy Director (Matilda da Rui), hiring more, plus volunteers.
orgs.caution: A distinct UK operation with its own staff, site, jobs and donation route — not simply a page of PauseAI Global. Chapter activity is uneven; the newer chapters are very new.

orgs.name: StopAI
orgs.the_ask: A permanent, enforceable global ban on all further development of frontier AI, plus citizen oversight bodies empowered to regulate or dismantle dangerous technologies.
orgs.what_they_do: Three fronts: public awareness, legislative influence, and non-violent direct action. Its own history page documents sit-ins inside OpenAI offices, a road blockade in front of OpenAI, banner drops and repeated protests at OpenAI and Microsoft since 2024.
orgs.newcomer_action: Attend an event from its Luma calendar, or attend the court proceedings of member Wynd Kaufmyn in San Francisco (it asks local supporters to show up in red shirts); donate.
orgs.geography: Primarily San Francisco Bay Area; one protest documented in Kinshasa, DRC.
orgs.scale: Very small — a core of activists, not a staffed organisation. No published budget or headcount.
orgs.caution: This is a civil-disobedience group and you should join only knowing that. Members have blockaded OpenAI's doors and been prosecuted: member Wynd Kaufmyn faced four misdemeanour charges (case CRI-25404422, San Francisco Superior Court), was denied the necessity defence, and the site states she was due to surrender to serve a sentence on 14 Aug 2026. It also subpoenaed Sam Altman (quashed). Its platform is broader than AI risk — it includes rejecting transhumanism and AI personhood, calls for a smaller economy, and bans on AI weapons. Not all actions are legal; attending a protest can carry arrest risk.

orgs.name: Encode (formerly Encode Justice; also Encode AI)
orgs.the_ask: Pass enforceable AI laws — transparency, safety frameworks, incident reporting, third-party audits and whistleblower protection for frontier AI companies — while keeping AI's benefits.
orgs.what_they_do: Legislative drafting and advocacy. Claims credit for California SB 53, the New York RAISE Act, Illinois SB 315, the federal TAKE IT DOWN Act, and the first US policy on AI in nuclear weapons launch. Builds coalitions and lobbies directly.
orgs.newcomer_action: Email info@encodeai.org offering your skill (law, policy research, state-level organising), follow @EncodeAction, and donate.
orgs.scale: Small: at least 11 staff listed on its team page; describes itself as 'a small advocacy team'.
orgs.caution: encodejustice.org now redirects to encodeai.org — the youth-chapter branding of Encode Justice has largely been folded into a professional policy shop. Its current site advertises no chapters, no volunteer programme and no membership, so a newcomer's realistic route is donating or being hired, not joining. Its ask is regulation and transparency, explicitly 'pro-human pro-AI' — not a pause or ban.

orgs.name: The Midas Project
orgs.the_ask: AI companies should keep the safety and transparency commitments they have publicly made, and be held accountable when they quietly walk them back.
orgs.what_they_do: Corporate watchdog work: the Watchtower tracker of silent changes to AI company policies, investigations, scorecards, and the OpenAI Files. Runs modelrepublic.org and openaifiles.org.
orgs.newcomer_action: Send a tip if you have inside knowledge of an AI company; otherwise sign up as a volunteer, join the Discord and help with research or amplifying campaigns.
orgs.tips: yes — dedicated tip page at themidasproject.com/tips, aimed at industry insiders
orgs.scale: Tiny: founded early 2024 by Tyler Johnston, 'a small core team' plus volunteers. 501(c)(3), EIN 99-2326977.
orgs.caution: Adversarial toward specific named companies. If you work at an AI lab, sending a tip may breach your employment agreement — take legal advice first; the organisation is small and cannot indemnify you.

orgs.name: Center for AI Policy (CAIP)
orgs.the_ask: US federal government should build the capacity to see and respond to frontier AI risk — monitoring, standards and emergency powers.
orgs.what_they_do: Largely ceased. Its own homepage states 'CAIP has run out of funding and has ceased most of our active operations.' Two residual services continue: a grassroots Policy Advocacy Network training AI safety leaders, and free expert feedback on pending legislation.
orgs.newcomer_action: Little to join. If you are drafting AI legislation you can still request free review; if you are a funder, it invites contact about reviving the organisation.
orgs.scale: Effectively dormant. Last substantive publication dated 22 May 2025.
orgs.spending: Ran out of funding — that is the organisation's own stated reason for closing.
orgs.caution: FLAG: mostly closed. Do not plan effort around it. Revival contact given on its site is jason@aipolicy.us. This is also a useful data point about the funding asymmetry in this field.

orgs.name: Center for AI Safety Action Fund (CAIS AF)
orgs.the_ask: US policy should maintain American leadership in AI while protecting against AI-related national security threats — chip manufacturing leadership, compute security, preventing malicious use, and global cooperation on safe AI.
orgs.what_they_do: 501(c)(4) advocacy: convening lawmakers, business leaders and security experts; building bipartisan consensus; educating policymakers. Sister organisation to the Center for AI Safety research nonprofit.
orgs.newcomer_action: Donate (not tax-deductible), or apply for a job. There is no constituent action tool — this is an inside-Washington operation.
orgs.scale: Small professional policy staff. EIN 93-2442608.
orgs.spending: Not published on its own site; a 501(c)(4) so donations are not tax-deductible and donors need not be disclosed.
orgs.caution: Its framing is national-security and US competitiveness, not a pause or ban — noticeably more hawkish in framing than PauseAI or ControlAI, and it sits comfortably with 'US leadership in AI'. If your goal is slowing AI, check the framing matches your intent. There is essentially no public participation route.

orgs.name: Future of Life Institute (FLI)
orgs.the_ask: A moratorium on developing artificial superintelligence for at least 15 years, plus licensing, auditing and enforceable safety standards before scaling — and a participatory global process rather than decisions made by a handful of CEOs.
orgs.what_they_do: Open letters and petitions (Pause Giant AI Experiments, 31,810 signatories; Asilomar AI Principles), a contact-your-legislator tool, EU AI Act implementation work, grantmaking, the Digital Media Accelerator, and a newsletter with about 70,000 subscribers. It is a registered lobbying entity in both the US and EU.
orgs.newcomer_action: Use the contact-your-legislator tool, sign the open letters, join the action alerts list, or apply to the Digital Media Accelerator if you make creative content.
orgs.geography: United States and European Union (Brussels lobbying presence).
orgs.scale: Mid-sized and well-funded by the standards of this field; a large grantmaker as well as an advocate.
orgs.spending: Registers as a federal lobbying client in the US (OpenSecrets ID D000087562) and appears on the EU transparency register; specific figures not retrieved from its own pages.
orgs.caution: FLI does not have a separately branded advocacy arm — its policy and lobbying work runs through the Institute itself plus EU-registered activity. Its ask is a time-limited moratorium on superintelligence, which is weaker than ControlAI's or StopAI's permanent ban and stronger than Encode's transparency agenda. It is also a funder of other groups on this list, so 'independent' endorsements between these organisations are not always independent.

orgs.name: Existential Risk Observatory
orgs.the_ask: Raise public awareness of existential risks — above all unaligned AI — because public understanding is the precondition for policy that reduces them.
orgs.what_they_do: Media work, op-eds, public debate and campaign work across AI, engineered pandemics, extreme climate scenarios and nuclear war; research and policy specialists on staff.
orgs.newcomer_action: Read and share its output and contact the team directly; there is no published one-click action page.
orgs.scale: Around 15+ people listed including researchers, campaign managers and policy specialists — several affiliated with the University of Groningen.
orgs.caution: Awareness-raising rather than a campaign you can join. Its donate and get-involved pages could not be retrieved, so treat any volunteering or giving route as UNVERIFIED and email first. Its remit is broader than AI.

orgs.name: CAES — Collective Action for Existential Safety (Center for Existential Safety)
orgs.the_ask: Individuals, organisations and nations should each take concrete personal action on existential risk — from AI, nuclear weapons and engineered pandemics — starting today.
orgs.what_they_do: Runs a structured action plan with separate tracks for individuals, organisations and nations, a 30-second quiz that routes you to a first action, a commitment tracker, a Discord community, and a pledge site. Curates other groups' actions rather than lobbying itself.
orgs.newcomer_action: Take the quiz on the homepage, tick five commitments in the action tracker, sign the Existential Safety Action Pledge and join the Discord.
orgs.tips: no — but it takes suggestions for missing actions via an Airtable form
orgs.scale: Very small. Copyright notice reads 'Center for Existential Safety'; the pledge site lists only a handful of public signatories (including James Norris). Treat as a small project, not an institution.
orgs.caution: The pledge is demanding: signers commit to 'take at least one action every workday to reduce existential risks until an international body of recognized experts has declared humanity's risk of extinction is under 0.1% per year'. Read that before signing. The site is a directory that points to other organisations — useful as a front door, but joining CAES is not the same as joining a campaign with staff and legislative access.

orgs.name: Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI)
orgs.the_ask: A globally coordinated and collectively enforced moratorium on the development of artificial superintelligence, because on current methods the most likely outcome is human extinction.
orgs.what_they_do: Since 2024 primarily a communications and advocacy organisation rather than a technical lab: the book 'If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies', the AI StopWatch daily news service, a documentary, and a contact-your-representative tool run off the book's site.
orgs.newcomer_action: Use ifanyonebuildsit.com/act to call, email or post a letter to your representative asking them to push for an international pause; add your name to the pledge to march in Washington DC (the march is contingent on reaching 100,000 pledges).
orgs.geography: United States primarily (the contact tool finds US representatives); global readership.
orgs.scale: Small research-and-comms nonprofit, long-established (founded 2000), donor-funded.
orgs.spending: Not disclosed on the pages checked; accepts donations.
orgs.caution: MIRI's stated position is that building superintelligence with current techniques most likely kills everyone. That is the strongest claim on this list; endorsing it publicly has social and professional costs in some workplaces. The DC march is conditional and may never happen.

orgs.name: SaferAI
orgs.the_ask: AI companies should be held to real risk-management standards, and governance should be built on rigorous, auditable frameworks rather than voluntary promises.
orgs.what_they_do: Research on risk management frameworks, public ratings of AI companies' safety practices (ratings.safer-ai.org), and standards work in EU and international governance processes.
orgs.newcomer_action: Read and cite the company ratings when arguing with policymakers or employers; donate; apply for an open role.
orgs.geography: France (Paris) and EU-level; registered French nonprofit, reg. no. 919 185 199 00016.
orgs.scale: Small technical nonprofit; headcount not published.
orgs.caution: A research and standards body, not a campaign — there is no membership or activist route. Its ratings are useful ammunition for other people's campaigns.

orgs.name: AI Safety Asia (AISA)
orgs.the_ask: Asian institutions — especially Southeast Asian and middle-power states — should have real leverage over how frontier AI is built and governed, before the terms are locked in by a handful of dominant actors.
orgs.what_they_do: Three programmes: Curate (helps governments map AI dependencies and connect to frontier-risk scientists), Inform (translates technical foresight into safeguards for negotiations), Catalyse (maintains channels between senior officials across bridge states). Listed by UNESCO as a civil society organisation and by the World Economic Forum.
orgs.newcomer_action: Subscribe to the AI governance briefing newsletter; if you are a policymaker, researcher or organisation working on AI governance in Asia, email contact@aisafety.asia.
orgs.geography: Asia, with emphasis on Southeast Asia and middle powers.
orgs.scale: Small; headcount not disclosed. Non-profit.
orgs.spending: Not disclosed; no donation page found.
orgs.caution: Aimed at officials and researchers, not the general public — the get-involved page explicitly invites policymakers, researchers and organisations. If you are none of those, the newsletter is realistically your only route. No verified donation route.

orgs.name: Concordia AI
orgs.the_ask: Build AI safety capacity and international coordination in and with China — better risk monitoring, standards input and cross-border dialogue.
orgs.what_they_do: Research, convenings, consulting to AI labs on risk management, contributions to Chinese national AI standards and policy consultations, and frontier risk monitoring across cyber, bio, chemical and manipulation domains. Runs the AI Risk Monitor and the State of AI Safety in China reports.
orgs.newcomer_action: Subscribe to the AI Safety in China newsletter (aisafetychina.substack.com) and read the State of AI Safety reports; apply for a job if you have relevant expertise.
orgs.geography: China (Beijing) and Singapore, with global engagement.
orgs.scale: Small; headcount not disclosed. Note it describes itself as a 'social enterprise', not a charity.
orgs.spending: Commercial consulting revenue; no donation route.
orgs.caution: It is a social enterprise that consults for AI companies, so it is not a disinterested campaigner and takes no donations or volunteers. There is no advocacy route for a member of the public — its value to you is information.

orgs.name: Americans for Responsible Innovation (ARI)
orgs.the_ask: The US government should take a proactive approach to AI governance that protects the public, including preserving states' ability to regulate AI rather than pre-empting them.
orgs.what_they_do: Policy research, reports and briefs; federal advocacy; and since September 2026 a nationwide push for state-level AI guardrails. Cofounded by former Rep. Brad Carson, who also leads the Public First super PAC network.
orgs.newcomer_action: Join the email list for policy updates, read Policy Bytes, and donate via Support Us; contact staff if you can help on a state campaign.
orgs.geography: United States — federal and, since 2026, state legislatures.
orgs.scale: Established think-tank/advocacy hybrid with professional staff; headcount not published on its site.
orgs.spending: Not disclosed on its own site. Reported by Forbes as funded by effective-altruism-linked donors and safety-focused investors, and connected to the pro-regulation super PAC effort — treat that attribution as UNVERIFIED against ARI's own pages.
orgs.caution: No explicit volunteer or membership programme on its site — the realistic newcomer routes are the mailing list and money. Its leadership overlap with the Public First super PACs means supporting ARI is adjacent to electoral politics, which some people will not want.

orgs.name: Secure AI Project
orgs.the_ask: Adopt policies that reduce the risk of severe harm from advanced AI, built on transparency, accountability and safe development.
orgs.what_they_do: Drafts and advocates for specific bills — notably associated with California SB 53 — and publishes a list of bills it supports. Staff include Thomas Woodside.
orgs.newcomer_action: Read the 'bills we support' page, then write to your California or federal legislator citing it; donate; contact them if you have drafting or technical expertise.
orgs.geography: United States, with a strong California state focus. Address: 584 Castro Street #3160, San Francisco.
orgs.scale: Very small. Its own site names no team, which is itself a signal about size.
orgs.caution: Its own website discloses no team, no board and no budget — you would be donating to an organisation whose scale is not public. Its ask is targeted transparency legislation, not a pause.

orgs.name: The Future Society
orgs.the_ask: Align AI through better governance — workable international rules, EU implementation, and AI security policy, rather than leaving frontier development ungoverned.
orgs.what_they_do: Policy research and direct engagement with US, European and international decision-makers on international AI governance, European AI governance and AI security; publishes on verification, compute capacity, AI-enabled weapons, risk standards and agent regulation.
orgs.newcomer_action: Read its resource library and cite it in consultation responses; donate; apply for one of its remote European analyst roles.
orgs.scale: Small-to-mid policy nonprofit; salary bands published ($58.4K–$99.2K) suggest a modest budget.
orgs.caution: An insider policy shop. No campaign, no volunteering, no petitions — if you want to *do* something rather than fund or join it professionally, look elsewhere.

orgs.name: Center for Humane Technology
orgs.the_ask: Change the incentives driving AI deployment, and establish new norms, legal protections and fundamental rights to preserve what makes human life meaningful in the age of AI.
orgs.what_they_do: Public education (the Your Undivided Attention podcast, The AI Dilemma talk, a free course), a policy reforms toolkit, and the 'AI and What Makes Us Human' initiative; works with decision-makers on systems-level interventions.
orgs.newcomer_action: Take the free course and use the Policy Reforms toolkit to brief a local official, employer or school; subscribe to the Substack.
orgs.scale: Mid-sized nonprofit with a fellowship programme and well-known founders (Tristan Harris, Aza Raskin).
orgs.caution: Framing is attention economy, mental health and social harm rather than extinction risk, though it covers both. High-profile media presence; less legislative throughput than Encode or Secure AI Project.

orgs.name: Common Sense Media
orgs.the_ask: Children should be protected from unsafe AI — independent risk ratings for AI products, and states must keep the power to pass their own children's AI safety laws.
orgs.what_they_do: Independent risk assessments of AI products (rating Google Search AI, ChatGPT-5, Grok, Perplexity, Claude and AI mental health apps from 'Moderate Risk' to 'Unacceptable Risk'); research on teen AI use; campaigns against the executive order blocking state AI laws; work on deepfakes, AI toys and AI companions.
orgs.newcomer_action: Sign the petition challenging the executive order blocking state AI laws; check the AI ratings before your child uses a tool; subscribe to the newsletters.
orgs.geography: United States, with strong California state activity.
orgs.scale: Large and well-established — by far the biggest child-safety-focused organisation on this list, with its own research institute.
orgs.spending: Not disclosed on the pages checked; accepts donations.
orgs.caution: Its frame is child safety and product harm, not catastrophic or existential risk. Broad public appeal but a narrower ask than the pause/ban groups — a good fit if your concern is kids and chatbots, a poor one if it is frontier capability.

orgs.name: Campaign to Stop Killer Robots
orgs.the_ask: A new international treaty on autonomy in weapons systems, to ensure meaningful human control over the use of force.
orgs.what_they_do: Coalition campaigning: petitions, a parliamentary pledge, research and monitoring, and diplomatic advocacy at the UN. Steering committee includes Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International, Article 36, ICRAC, Mines Action Canada, PAX and SEHLAC.
orgs.newcomer_action: Sign the petition and use the 'get politicians involved' tool to ask your MP or representative to sign the parliamentary pledge; join the newsletter.
orgs.scale: Large coalition, small secretariat. 20,000+ petition signatures and 150+ parliamentary pledge signatories by its own count.
orgs.spending: Not disclosed; accepts donations and organisational membership.
orgs.caution: Covers autonomous weapons specifically, not general AI risk. If you belong to an organisation (a union branch, faith group, NGO), it will sign that organisation up as a member — the highest-leverage thing most people can do here.

orgs.name: Public First Action / Public First PAC
orgs.the_ask: Elect and pressure federal and state politicians to back AI safeguards for children, workers and the public, stronger semiconductor export controls, and transparency from leading AI labs — and to resist federal pre-emption of state AI laws.
orgs.what_they_do: A 501(c)(4) plus three affiliated super PACs (Public First PAC, Jobs and Democracy PAC, Defending Our Values PAC). Led by former Reps. Chris Stewart (R-Utah) and Brad Carson (D-Okla.). This is the pro-safeguards electoral counterweight to Leading the Future.
orgs.newcomer_action: Donate to whichever entity fits your politics, or fill in the questionnaire to make contact; candidates can seek its endorsement.
orgs.geography: United States — federal and state races.
orgs.scale: New (2025-26) and small relative to the industry PACs.
orgs.spending: Reported by Forbes as expecting to raise at least $50 million for the 2026 cycle, against Leading the Future's $100M+ launch — roughly a 1:2 to 1:3 disadvantage before Meta's separate spending is counted. Figure is third-party; treat as UNVERIFIED against its own filings.
orgs.caution: This is partisan electoral money on both sides of the aisle, not charity — donations are not tax-deductible and will be spent attacking and supporting candidates. Reported to be backed by Anthropic employees and executives, which means an AI company's staff are funding one side of the AI safety fight; weigh that.

orgs.name: AI Money Watch (a project of Demand Progress)
orgs.the_ask: Make AI industry political spending visible, so voters can see who is paying for which candidate.
orgs.what_they_do: A public tracker of AI-related political spending built from FEC independent expenditure filings, updated daily, browsable by candidate, race and funder, with a published methodology.
orgs.newcomer_action: Look up your own district before you vote or donate, and send the funder page to your local journalist or representative.
orgs.scale: A project of Demand Progress, a long-running grassroots democracy organisation; the tracker itself is small.
orgs.spending: Demand Progress accepts donations via ActBlue.
orgs.caution: Demand Progress's own homepage does not list AI as a focus area — AI Money Watch is a discrete project, so do not assume donating to Demand Progress funds AI work. The tracker's figures ($75.5M raised by Leading the Future, ~$70M cash on hand as of January 2026) come from FEC filings and will differ from press reports of total pledged commitments.

orgs.name: Leading the Future
orgs.the_ask: Elect politicians who will keep AI lightly regulated, and secure a single federal framework that pre-empts state AI laws.
orgs.what_they_do: Super PAC network formed 15 August 2025, led by Zac Moffatt (R) and Josh Vlasto (D). Endorses and spends in both parties' primaries; affiliated vehicles include Build American AI (advocacy nonprofit), American Mission PAC and Think Big PAC. Targeted New York Assemblymember Alex Bores, author of the RAISE Act.
orgs.newcomer_action: Nothing to join — this is the opposition. Look up its spending in your race on AI Money Watch before you vote or volunteer for a candidate.
orgs.geography: United States — federal and increasingly state races.
orgs.scale: Very large relative to every safety organisation on this list combined.
orgs.spending: $100M+ at launch; over $140 million raised per public reporting, with Andreessen Horowitz alone above $50 million by April 2026; FEC-derived tracker shows $75.5M raised and ~$70M cash on hand in January 2026. Funders reported to include a16z, OpenAI president Greg Brockman, Joe Lonsdale and Perplexity.
orgs.caution: UNVERIFIED against the PAC's own site — figures here come from Wikipedia, Forbes, CNBC and the FEC-based AI Money Watch tracker, and 'raised', 'pledged' and 'cash on hand' are different numbers that press coverage often conflates. Reported controversies include an AI-generated news site using fake journalist personas (April 2026), $5,000-per-video payments to influencers pushing a China-threat message (May 2026), and an FEC complaint over shell-company payments (May 2026) — all allegations reported by third parties.

orgs.name: Build American AI
orgs.the_ask: Shift public opinion toward AI deregulation and a federal framework pre-empting state laws.
orgs.what_they_do: The advocacy/dark-money arm of Leading the Future, led by Nathan Leamer; runs paid public-opinion campaigns. Reported to deliberately steer debate away from technical safety questions.
orgs.newcomer_action: Nothing to join. If you see AI ads in your area, check whether they are Build American AI's before assuming they are grassroots.
orgs.scale: Well-funded ad operation.
orgs.caution: UNVERIFIED against its own site — figures from Forbes and Wikipedia. As a 501(c)(4) it does not disclose donors, so 'who is paying for this ad' is not answerable from public filings.

orgs.name: American Technology Excellence Project (Meta)
orgs.the_ask: Stop states passing their own AI and tech rules; replace the 'patchwork' with a single permissive national approach.
orgs.what_they_do: Meta's bipartisan super PAC, announced 23 September 2025, aimed squarely at state-level AI legislation and state races.
orgs.newcomer_action: Nothing to join. If you are lobbying a state legislator on AI, expect this money to be on the other side of the conversation.
orgs.geography: United States — state elections, with heavy California activity.
orgs.scale: Large.
orgs.spending: Announced as 'tens of millions'; subsequent reporting describes a roughly $65 million election push in 2026.
orgs.caution: UNVERIFIED against Meta's own filings — figures from Axios, TechRepublic and GV Wire. This is separate from and additional to Leading the Future, so the two should not be added together casually, but they do point the same way.

orgs.name: TechNet
orgs.the_ask: Congress should pass a narrow, risk-based federal AI framework that pre-empts state AI laws, without private rights of action or mandatory independent audits.
orgs.what_they_do: Trade association lobbying for major AI developers and deployers; state and federal advocacy; runs the AI for America campaign (ai4america.com). Its own policy page states that 'federal preemption of state laws and regulations is needed to prevent a patchwork'.
orgs.newcomer_action: Nothing to join unless you are a company. Read its stated positions before a state hearing — it is usually the most organised voice in the room opposing state AI bills.
orgs.geography: United States — federal and all major state capitals.
orgs.scale: Large, professionally staffed trade association with state directors.
orgs.spending: Not published on its own site.
orgs.caution: Stated fairly: TechNet is not anti-safety in its own framing — it supports the voluntary NIST AI Risk Management Framework and sector-specific laws. What it actively opposes is state-level binding rules, private lawsuits and mandatory audits. Its member list is at technet.org/our-story/members/.

orgs.name: Consumer Technology Association (CTA)
orgs.the_ask: A national AI regulatory framework that is technology-neutral and risk-based and builds on existing law, rather than new rules that it says would hinder innovation and small businesses.
orgs.what_they_do: Trade association for consumer technology (organiser of CES); files policy comments on AI and lobbies federally.
orgs.newcomer_action: Nothing to join unless you are a company. Read its AI policy filings to see the industry's formal legal arguments in your own words.
orgs.scale: Very large, long-established trade association.
orgs.spending: Not published on the pages checked.
orgs.caution: CTA's own advocacy page does not explicitly state a position on federal pre-emption of state laws, though it has signed broader industry pre-emption coalition letters — treat any claim that CTA demands pre-emption as UNVERIFIED unless you find it in a specific filing.

orgs.name: Chamber of Progress
orgs.the_ask: Keep AI development and AI-generated work legally unencumbered — defend fair use for AI training, oppose broad restrictions on automated decision systems, and pursue a centre-left 'AI opportunity' agenda.
orgs.what_they_do: Center-left tech industry coalition. Runs the State AI Leadership Project (state-level advocacy), Generate & Create (defending AI training as fair use), the Democratic AI Opportunity Agenda, and the Progress Defense Fund for litigation. Opposed California SB 947.
orgs.newcomer_action: Nothing to join — it is a corporate coalition. If you are arguing about AI and copyright, its Generate & Create material is the clearest statement of the industry's position.
orgs.geography: United States — federal, state and courts.
orgs.scale: Mid-sized, staffed coalition with a litigation arm.
orgs.spending: Corporate funders are not disclosed on the homepage.
orgs.caution: Presents itself as progressive and center-left, which can make it read as civil society rather than industry — it is funded by tech companies and litigates on their side. If you are a writer, artist or musician, its copyright position is directly opposed to yours.

orgs.name: INCOMPAS
orgs.the_ask: Clear the way for AI infrastructure — faster siting and permitting for data centres, fibre, subsea cables and power — under 'responsible and innovative AI policy'.
orgs.what_they_do: Trade association rebranded as 'The Competitive Communications and AI Infrastructure Association'; runs an Artificial Intelligence Competition Center and lobbies on infrastructure, siting and energy.
orgs.newcomer_action: Nothing to join unless your company is a member. If you are fighting a local data centre, this is the association arguing the other side at state and federal level.
orgs.scale: Mid-sized trade association with a published member list.
orgs.caution: Its AI interest is infrastructure and competition, not model capability — on frontier safety questions it is mostly absent. The concrete conflict is local: data centre siting, water and electricity.

orgs.name: Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF)
orgs.the_ask: Regulate how AI is used — surveillance, algorithmic decisions, age-gating, encryption and competition — rather than restricting the technology itself; keep AI tools available and competitive.
orgs.what_they_do: Litigation, legislative advocacy and technical analysis across eight AI topics: algorithmic decision-making, AI and fair use, AI and surveillance, deepfakes/NCII, age-gating, privacy, encryption and competition. Runs an action centre with alerts to Congress and state legislatures.
orgs.newcomer_action: Take a live action at act.eff.org, and if you have a legal problem involving AI or surveillance, submit it through the legal assistance page.
orgs.tips: yes — legal assistance intake at eff.org/pages/legal-assistance; EFF reviews referrals but takes few cases
orgs.geography: United States primarily, with international policy work.
orgs.scale: Large: decades-old, with staff lawyers, technologists and activists.
orgs.spending: Member-funded nonprofit; accepts donations and has a membership scheme.
orgs.caution: EFF is explicitly sceptical of broad AI regulation and of some safety-motivated proposals, and defends fair use for AI training. If your ask is 'slow AI down', EFF is not your ally on that point even though it is a genuine civil liberties organisation. It cannot take most cases referred to it.

orgs.name: Electronic Privacy Information Center (EPIC)
orgs.the_ask: AI systems used on people — in policing, hiring, housing, healthcare, insurance and government — must be transparent, tested and accountable, and discriminatory screening and scoring tools should not be used.
orgs.what_they_do: Legal and policy advocacy across seven AI areas including AI in law enforcement, chatbot harms, commercial AI use, government AI use, risk assessments and screening/scoring. Files comments, complaints and amicus briefs; maintains a public digital library of AI documents.
orgs.newcomer_action: Search its digital library for the agency or company you are dealing with, then contact Calli Schroeder (Senior Counsel, AI & Human Rights Director) via the contact page if you have a concrete case.
orgs.tips: unclear — no published tip line; contact page is the only route
orgs.scale: Mid-sized, lawyer-heavy nonprofit.
orgs.caution: No public intake form for complaints — do not assume a tip will be acted on. Its focus is harm to identifiable people from deployed systems, not frontier or catastrophic risk.

orgs.name: Public Citizen
orgs.the_ask: Treat generative AI as a present danger: block federal deregulation and pre-emption of state AI laws, stop non-consensual AI images, and halt unchecked data centre build-out.
orgs.what_they_do: Consumer advocacy, litigation and petitions. Live campaigns include a petition against congressional AI deregulation, a petition on non-consensual AI images, and a letter urging a Texas data centre moratorium.
orgs.newcomer_action: Sign the petition against congressional AI deregulation (act.citizen.org/page/83712/petition/1) — it takes two minutes — and join the updates list.
orgs.tips: unclear — no dedicated AI whistleblower line found
orgs.scale: Large, long-established (founded 1971) with lobbying, litigation and research arms.
orgs.caution: Frames AI harm as consumer, labour and democratic harm happening now — it is generally dismissive of framing centred on future superintelligence. If you arrived via extinction-risk arguments, expect a different vocabulary.

orgs.name: Access Now
orgs.the_ask: AI must be governed by binding, enforceable rules rooted in international human rights law — transparent, accountable and in the public interest — with particular scrutiny of biometric surveillance and AI in warfare.
orgs.what_they_do: Global digital rights advocacy, research (including 'Bodily harms: how AI and biometrics curtail human rights'), UN and EU policy work, opposition to autonomous weapons, and the RightsCon conference. Runs a 24/7 Digital Security Helpline.
orgs.newcomer_action: If you are an activist, journalist or human rights defender facing a digital threat, open a case with the Digital Security Helpline; otherwise read and share its AI issue page.
orgs.tips: yes — the Digital Security Helpline takes cases 24/7 from at-risk users worldwide
orgs.scale: Large international NGO.
orgs.caution: Its position is rights-based governance, not bans on AI development. The helpline is for people at risk, not a general complaints line — do not clog it with policy questions.

orgs.name: Consumer Reports
orgs.the_ask: AI products sold to consumers should be tested, transparent and accountable, and states should keep their role in regulating AI.
orgs.what_they_do: Independent product testing plus a policy arm (CR Advocacy) that files regulatory comments, testifies to Congress (including on AI-enabled fraud and scams), surveys consumers on AI, and backs state algorithmic accountability bills such as Washington SB 5116. It publicly backed the Senate vote upholding states' role over AI regulation and raised concerns about the White House AI Action Plan.
orgs.newcomer_action: Read the CR Advocacy AI press releases to see which bills it supports, cite its testing in a complaint, and subscribe for advocacy alerts.
orgs.scale: Very large and well-resourced; one of the few AI-engaged organisations with its own independent testing labs.
orgs.spending: Subscription and donation funded; takes no advertising.
orgs.caution: Its AI landing page URL could not be confirmed — the domain and its AI positions are verified through CR's own press releases and research posts on advocacy.consumerreports.org, but treat any specific AI sub-page path as UNVERIFIED. Its focus is consumer protection, not catastrophic risk.

orgs.name: Which?
orgs.the_ask: Consumers should be protected in digital markets and against fraud, including AI-enabled scams.
orgs.what_they_do: UK consumer champion: product testing, consumer rights guidance, policy and insight work across nine areas including Digital Markets, Fraud and Consumer Insight, and a Scam Alerts service.
orgs.newcomer_action: Subscribe to Scam Alerts and read the AI scams guidance; if you want to influence policy, respond to its Consumer Insight Tracker work or contact its policy team.
orgs.tips: unclear — it runs a Scam Alerts service but a public AI-harm reporting tool was not confirmed
orgs.scale: Large, long-established consumer organisation with its own testing labs.
orgs.caution: FLAG: Which? has no dedicated AI policy programme that could be verified on its own site — AI appears inside fraud and digital markets work. If AI is your issue, this is a weaker route in the UK than approaching an MP directly or going through PauseAI UK or ControlAI.

orgs.name: BEUC (European Consumer Organisation)
orgs.the_ask: The EU AI Act must give consumers real, enforceable rights — accountability, transparency and control over AI — and must not be hollowed out by the digital omnibus deregulation.
orgs.what_they_do: Umbrella body for 44 independent national consumer organisations in 31 countries; lobbies EU institutions, files joint letters (e.g. July 2026 on keeping medical devices in the AI Act's scope) and publicly warned in May 2026 that the adopted AI omnibus 'risks creating dangerous regulatory loopholes and weakening consumer protection'.
orgs.newcomer_action: Join or contact your own national consumer organisation (the BEUC member in your country) — that is the only individual route; BEUC itself works with institutions, not individuals.
orgs.tips: no — complaints go to national member organisations
orgs.geography: European Union / Europe — 44 member organisations, 31 countries.
orgs.scale: Mid-sized Brussels secretariat representing very large national members.
orgs.spending: Member-funded and EU-grant funded; registered on the EU transparency register.
orgs.caution: BEUC does not take individual cases. Its influence is real but institutional; your leverage is through your national member organisation's campaigns.

orgs.name: Algorithmic Justice League (AJL)
orgs.the_ask: Stop AI harms and bias — especially from facial recognition and biometric systems — by centring the people most affected and giving them a way to report what happened to them.
orgs.what_they_do: Research, art and advocacy founded by Joy Buolamwini; runs report.ajl.org to collect public accounts of AI harm, campaigns such as #FreedomFlyers on TSA facial recognition, and equips advocates with empirical research.
orgs.newcomer_action: If an AI system has harmed you — a facial recognition misidentification, an airport scan, a rejected application — file it at report.ajl.org this week. Otherwise take an action from the Take Action page.
orgs.tips: yes — report.ajl.org is an explicit public harm-reporting channel
orgs.scale: Small organisation with very large cultural reach (Coded Bias, Buolamwini's research).
orgs.spending: Donations via ActBlue and merchandise sales.
orgs.caution: Its remit is bias, biometrics and civil rights harm, not frontier model risk. Reporting a harm is not legal representation — AJL is not a law firm and cannot act on your case.

orgs.name: AI Now Institute
orgs.the_ask: Challenge the current trajectory of AI by confronting industry concentration and power — antitrust scrutiny, limits on data centre expansion, and worker protection — rather than accepting scale as inevitable.
orgs.what_they_do: Independent research and policy analysis; maps the AI market and the industry's sources of power; publishes data centre policy toolkits and labour research (including AI in nursing); testifies to Congress (Monopoly Busters Caucus, Senate Banking Committee); investigates AI security incidents.
orgs.newcomer_action: Use its data centre policy toolkit if there is a proposed facility near you; cite its market-power research in submissions; apply for a role.
orgs.scale: Small research institute, co-led by Amba Kak and Sarah Myers West; high influence per head.
orgs.caution: A research institute, not a campaign — there is no petition, no membership and no volunteering. Its critique targets AI companies' power and is often explicitly at odds with the existential-risk framing used by groups like MIRI and ControlAI.

orgs.name: IEEE-USA AI Policy Committee (AIPC)
orgs.the_ask: US AI policy should be grounded in engineering reality: governance and regulation, safety, privacy and cybersecurity, IP protection, transparency, and a workforce pipeline matched to need.
orgs.what_they_do: Assembles IEEE members with AI expertise to write position statements reflecting consensus views of US-based members, which then guide IEEE-USA advocacy with Congress and federal agencies. The wider IEEE Standards Association runs the IEEE 7000 series of ethics-in-design standards and the Global Initiative on Ethics of Autonomous and Intelligent Systems.
orgs.newcomer_action: If you are an IEEE member, email the committee's programme manager (Erica Wissolik, e.wissolik@ieee.org) to ask how to join or contribute to a position statement; read the existing statements first.
orgs.volunteers: yes — via IEEE membership and the volunteer committees page
orgs.geography: United States (IEEE-USA); IEEE standards work is global.
orgs.scale: IEEE is the world's largest technical professional organisation; the AIPC itself is a small volunteer committee.
orgs.caution: Route in is membership — non-members have essentially no path. Consensus position statements are slow and deliberately moderate; if you want an organisation to say something urgent, this is not the vehicle. The committee page does not spell out the joining process, so email first.

orgs.name: ACM Technology Policy Council (with USTPC and Europe TPC)
orgs.the_ask: Generative AI and algorithmic systems should be built and deployed according to published principles covering safety, intellectual property, workforce impact, accountability, transparency and fairness.
orgs.what_they_do: Issues global and regional technology policy statements: the 'Principles for the Development, Deployment, and Use of Generative AI Technologies' (eight principles) and the joint US/Europe 'Statement on Principles for Responsible Algorithmic Systems' (nine principles). Provides nonpartisan technical briefings to policymakers. Chairs: James Hendler (TPC), Larry Medsker (USTPC), Chris Hankin (Europe TPC).
orgs.newcomer_action: If you are an ACM member, read the generative AI principles and contact the relevant committee about contributing; use the principles as a citable standard in your own workplace or submission.
orgs.geography: Global, with US and Europe committees.
orgs.scale: ACM is the largest computing professional society; the policy committees are small volunteer bodies with a small Washington office.
orgs.caution: The public policy pages do not explain how to volunteer for the committees — treat joining as UNVERIFIED and email the ACM Technology Policy Office. Principles are advisory and carry no enforcement.

orgs.name: American Medical Association (AMA)
orgs.the_ask: Health AI must be ethical, equitable and responsible: disclosed to physicians and patients, overseen by clinicians, with clear rules on physician liability, data privacy, and limits on payers' use of automated decision-making.
orgs.what_they_do: Sets formal AMA policy (searchable in PolicyFinder), publishes the AMA Principles for Augmented Intelligence Development, Deployment and Use, runs the AI Specialty Collaborative and STEPS Forward governance toolkits, surveys physician sentiment, and lobbies Congress on health AI including insurer use of AI in coverage decisions.
orgs.newcomer_action: If you are a physician: join the AI Specialty Collaborative through your specialty society, and use the STEPS Forward governance module to push your employer to adopt an AI policy. Bring a resolution through your state delegation if you want AMA policy changed.
orgs.volunteers: yes — through the House of Delegates and specialty societies, members only
orgs.scale: Very large, with one of the biggest health lobbying operations in Washington.
orgs.spending: Membership and publishing funded; a major federal lobbying spender.
orgs.caution: The AMA deliberately uses 'augmented intelligence' rather than 'artificial intelligence' to signal that AI should assist and not replace physicians — that framing is itself the position. Change happens through the House of Delegates resolution process, which is slow and requires membership and a sponsoring society.

orgs.name: British Medical Association (BMA)
orgs.the_ask: AI in the NHS must support and not supplant doctors, with clear principles for safe clinical use and protection of NHS patient data.
orgs.what_they_do: Publishes BMA Principles for Artificial Intelligence and its Application in Healthcare; responds to NHS plans (it has publicly opposed AI being used to supplant doctors in the NHS plan) and has warned about risks to NHS data from AI deals; represents doctors in negotiation and in the press.
orgs.newcomer_action: If you are a BMA member, read the AI principles document and raise AI in your local negotiating committee or through a motion to the Annual Representative Meeting.
orgs.volunteers: yes — members only, through BMA committee structures
orgs.scale: Large — the UK doctors' trade union and professional association.
orgs.caution: UNVERIFIED: the principles PDF URL is on the BMA's own domain but was located via search rather than fetched, and the 2026 positions cited (NHS plan, NHS data warnings) come from third-party reporting. Confirm on bma.org.uk before relying on it. Route in is membership.

orgs.name: National Education Association (NEA)
orgs.the_ask: AI in schools must be equitable, ethical and educator-led — with data privacy safeguards, rigorous vetting of tools for bias and effectiveness, and meaningful educator involvement in every adoption decision.
orgs.what_they_do: Adopted an AI policy statement and task force report; publishes vetting guides, a classroom AI glossary, accessibility and multilingual-learner guidance, micro-credentials in AI ethics and responsible use; provides sample school board resolutions and template letters to state education departments; runs an Action Center for advocacy.
orgs.newcomer_action: Take the sample school board resolution to your next board meeting, or send the template letter to your state department of education asking for a chief privacy officer and an AI vetting standard. Start a micro-credential.
orgs.scale: The largest labour union in the United States (roughly three million members).
orgs.spending: Membership funded; substantial state and federal lobbying.
orgs.caution: Its ask is governance of classroom AI, not restrictions on AI development. Its guidance has drawn political attack over equity provisions, so expect the school board conversation to be contested. Members-only routes.

orgs.name: American Federation of Teachers (AFT)
orgs.the_ask: AI's impact on the workplace should be a mandatory subject of collective bargaining, with contract language preventing worker displacement and a union seat at the table during development, procurement and implementation.
orgs.what_they_do: 2024 AI resolution; the 'Commonsense Guardrails for Using Advanced Technology in Schools' report; professional development and e-learning on AI; supports members bargaining AI clauses; calls for regulation on privacy, bias, misinformation and deepfakes and for respect for intellectual property.
orgs.newcomer_action: If you are an AFT member, propose AI language for your next contract using the resolution and guardrails report as the basis, and raise it with your local's bargaining team this week.
orgs.scale: Large national union (about 1.8 million members) covering teachers, higher education and healthcare staff.
orgs.caution: AFT's stance is 'responsible and principled development and use' — it is not anti-AI and has partnered with AI companies on teacher training, which some members object to. The bargaining route is the genuinely powerful one; the policy statements are not binding on employers by themselves.

orgs.name: SAG-AFTRA
orgs.the_ask: Performers must control their own voice and likeness: informed consent and compensation for digital replicas in contracts, and a federal right for all Americans to control their likeness and voice via the NO FAKES Act.
orgs.what_they_do: Negotiates AI terms into film, TV, commercial, audiobook and video game contracts; lobbies Congress and state legislatures (it backed California's law requiring disclosure of AI-generated performances in advertising); enforces contract terms for members.
orgs.newcomer_action: Sign the NO FAKES Act petition today (open to the public, not just members); if you are a member, report any unauthorised AI use of your voice or likeness to the union.
orgs.volunteers: yes — members through locals and committees
orgs.tips: yes — members can report contract violations to the union
orgs.scale: Large union (around 160,000 members) with real bargaining power and a proven willingness to strike over AI.
orgs.caution: Its ask is control and consent over likeness, not limits on AI capability. The NO FAKES Act is contested by some digital rights groups (including EFF) as a broad new IP right that could restrict speech — you are picking a side in that argument by signing.

orgs.name: Writers Guild of America (WGA West/East)
orgs.the_ask: AI cannot write or rewrite literary material, cannot be credited, and cannot be used to undermine writers' credit or compensation — terms won in the 2023 Minimum Basic Agreement after a 148-day strike.
orgs.what_they_do: Negotiates and enforces the MBA's AI provisions; maintains Know Your Rights guidance on AI; provides legal services to members; runs a violation reporting route.
orgs.newcomer_action: If you are a member and a studio used AI on your material, file through Report a Violation. If you are not, read the AI Know Your Rights page — it is the clearest published example of enforceable AI contract language anyone has won.
orgs.tips: yes — Report a Violation, members only
orgs.geography: United States (film, TV and new media).
orgs.scale: Mid-sized union with outsized leverage in its industry.
orgs.caution: Protections apply only to work covered by the MBA — non-union writing, and most AI training on already-published scripts, is not covered. Enforcement depends on writers actually reporting.

orgs.name: International Federation of Journalists (IFJ)
orgs.the_ask: AI in the media must serve ethically-produced journalism, comply with the Global Charter of Ethics, and be governed by negotiated standards rather than imposed by employers.
orgs.what_they_do: Issued IFJ Recommendations on the Use of Artificial Intelligence (June 2024) with global unions, and adopted a Global Framework Agreement on Artificial Intelligence in the Media (May 2026). Coordinates an AI working group across affiliated national unions.
orgs.newcomer_action: Join or contact your national journalists' union and ask them to apply the IFJ Recommendations in your next collective agreement — the IFJ works through affiliates, not individuals.
orgs.geography: Global — affiliates in 148+ countries representing about 600,000 journalists.
orgs.scale: Large federation, small secretariat.
orgs.caution: No individual membership — everything runs through your national union. Framework agreements are only as strong as each affiliate's ability to enforce them locally.

orgs.name: National Union of Journalists (NUJ)
orgs.the_ask: AI must not be used to cut journalism jobs or degrade editorial standards; its use should be negotiated with the union, with transparency and protection of journalists' work.
orgs.what_they_do: UK and Ireland journalists' union: chapel-level negotiation over AI in newsrooms, industrial action where AI is used to justify job losses (Mirror journalists balloted for strike action over AI-linked job threats), parliamentary work on AI in journalism, and an AI policy for members.
orgs.newcomer_action: If you are a journalist, join the NUJ and raise AI at your chapel; ask your employer for its AI policy in writing.
orgs.volunteers: yes — members only, through chapels and branches
orgs.scale: Mid-sized union (roughly 30,000 members).
orgs.caution: UNVERIFIED: the NUJ website blocked automated access, so the specific AI policy page URL and current wording could not be confirmed — only nuj.org.uk itself is given, and the 2026 industrial action is from third-party reporting (Personnel Today, Nieman Lab). Confirm directly. Route in is membership.

asia_latam.body: Standing Committee on Communications and Information Technology (Department-Related Parliamentary Standing Committee No. 18)
asia_latam.local_name: संचार और सूचना प्रौद्योगिकी संबंधी स्थायी समिति
asia_latam.ai_jurisdiction: Oversight of MeitY, Ministry of Communications and Ministry of Information & Broadcasting. Covers AI policy, IndiaAI Mission budgets, IT Rules, deepfakes/AI-generated content, data protection, telecom. It examines Demands for Grants and can self-select AI subjects; it has no power to amend rules, only to report.

chair.name: Nishikant Dubey
chair.role: Chairperson (BJP, Lok Sabha, Godda constituency)

asia_latam.current_business: 2025-26 committee (31 members: 21 Lok Sabha + 10 Rajya Sabha per current LS practice; PRS lists 28 as 20+8 — the exact count is disputed between sources, see note). Reported in March 2026 on the impact of the emergence of artificial intelligence. Also active on Make in India in electronics (meeting 25 June 2026), fake news/misinformation and telecom. VERIFIED that Dubey chaired as of June 2026 via ANI; committees are normally reconstituted each September, so a 2026-27 reconstitution may have occurred in the days around this date — re-check before citing.
asia_latam.public_route: Two routes. (1) When a committee takes up a subject or a Bill it issues a Press Communiqué through PIB and on sansad.in inviting memoranda from 'individuals, organisations, experts and stakeholders', usually 15-21 days, submitted by post or email to the Committee Branch, Lok Sabha Secretariat. (2) Writing directly to the Chairperson or the Committee's Director/Additional Director at any time. There is no standing online submission portal for DRSCs.
asia_latam.language: English and Hindi. Submissions accepted in either. No other languages served.
asia_latam.threshold: None. No signature or supporter threshold. Acceptance of a memorandum is entirely at the Chairperson's discretion, and there is no obligation to acknowledge or publish it.
asia_latam.realistic: Partly usable. An ordinary person can post or email a memorandum and it costs nothing, but there is no tracking, no acknowledgement and no publication of unsolicited submissions. Oral evidence invitations go almost exclusively to industry bodies, ministries and a small set of established think tanks. A non-Indian or an unaffiliated individual is very unlikely to be called. The realistic value is written input that may be cited anonymously in a report.
asia_latam.note: Chair verified via ANI reporting (June 2026) and PRS India committee page. The official sansad.in per-committee deep link returns HTTP 500 intermittently; the eParlib composition PDF for 2025-26 is at https://eparlib.sansad.in/bitstream/123456789/3017142/1/18_Communications_and_Information_Technology_25.pdf. Membership counts differ between PRS (28) and Lok Sabha rules (31) — treat as UNVERIFIED on that specific number.

asia_latam.body: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)
asia_latam.local_name: इलेक्ट्रॉनिकी और सूचना प्रौद्योगिकी मंत्रालय
asia_latam.ai_jurisdiction: The primary AI policy ministry. Owns the IndiaAI Mission, the India AI Governance Guidelines (Nov 2025), the IT Act and IT Rules including the 2026 AI-labelling/deepfake amendments, the DPDP Act rules, and the India AI Impact Summit. Any future Indian AI statute will originate here.

chair.name: Ashwini Vaishnaw
chair.role: Union Minister for Electronics and Information Technology (also Railways and Information & Broadcasting). Minister of State: Jitin Prasada. Secretary, MeitY: S. Krishnan.

asia_latam.current_business: Implementation of the India AI Governance Guidelines (released Nov 2025, foregrounded at the Feb 2026 Summit, 'seven sutras' framework). Operating the AIGEG/TPEC structure constituted 16 April 2026. Draft IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Second Amendment Rules 2026 on AI-generated content labelling — consultation ran 30 March to 29 April 2026 (extended from 14 April); notified thereafter. Reported to be studying a graded, risk-based AI law rather than a single AI Act.
asia_latam.public_route: MeitY does not use a single standing portal. Its actual mechanism is: it publishes a draft plus a one-page 'inviting comments' notice as a PDF under meity.gov.in/documents or /ministry/whats-new, and names a consultation-specific email address. Comments go to that address as .docx or .pdf. Some consultations are additionally mirrored on MyGov (mygov.in) as a 'Discussion' or 'Consultation' with a comment box. Worked example: the Draft IT Amendment Rules 2026 consultation took comments at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in, rule-by-rule, in MS Word or PDF, deadline extended to 29 April 2026.
asia_latam.language: English (Hindi notionally accepted; in practice all drafts and responses are in English).
asia_latam.threshold: None. Any person or organisation may email comments. India's Pre-Legislative Consultation Policy 2014 notionally requires 30 days, but MeitY has repeatedly used shorter windows and civil society (IFF, SFLC.in) has formally objected.
asia_latam.realistic: Genuinely usable, and one of the easier routes in this list — a single email with a PDF attached is the whole procedure. Two honest caveats: MeitY frequently states that submissions are 'held in fiduciary capacity' and will not be published, so you cannot see what others said or whether you were read; and windows are often short and announced with little notice. Set an alert on meity.gov.in/whats-new rather than expecting to be notified. Note that meity.gov.in is JavaScript-rendered, so its consultation listing does not load for simple scrapers or link-preview tools.
asia_latam.note: Consultation mechanism and the itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in address VERIFIED from the MeitY notice PDF at https://www.meity.gov.in/static/uploads/2026/04/964ca48ac7d0c92e3bba5d32d9a59fcb.pdf and corroborated by SFLC.in. As of 2026-09-22 I could not confirm an open consultation window; the most recent verified one closed 29 April 2026. The /documents/public-consultation landing URL is given as the standing entry point but renders client-side.

asia_latam.body: IndiaAI Mission (IndiaAI Independent Business Division)
asia_latam.local_name: इंडियाAI मिशन
asia_latam.ai_jurisdiction: Executing agency for India's national AI programme (approx. INR 10,372 crore). Seven pillars including Compute Capacity, Foundation Models, Datasets (AIKosh), Application Development, Future Skills, Startup Financing, and Safe & Trusted AI. Runs the compute tenders, GPU allocation, model-development grants, and the Safe & Trusted AI research portfolio.

chair.name: Saurabh Vijay
chair.role: Chief Executive Officer, IndiaAI Mission (IAS 1998, Maharashtra cadre; concurrently CEO, UIDAI). Chief Operating Officer: Sudeep Shrivastava, Joint Secretary, MeitY.

asia_latam.current_business: Structured as an Independent Business Division (IBD) of Digital India Corporation, a Section 8 company under MeitY — not a statutory body, which matters: its decisions are corporate/administrative, not subject to parliamentary rule-making scrutiny. As of July 2026, 13 projects approved under the Safe & Trusted AI pillar addressing deepfakes and bias. Nationwide AI skilling programme (target 1 million youth) launched January 2026.
asia_latam.public_route: No formal comment mechanism. Practical routes: (a) respond to its Expressions of Interest and calls for proposals published at indiaai.gov.in — these are open to academia, startups and non-profits and are the only route with a defined process; (b) general contact form/email on indiaai.gov.in; (c) reach it indirectly through a MeitY consultation.
asia_latam.language: English.
asia_latam.threshold: Calls for proposals impose eligibility thresholds — typically Indian-registered legal entity, sometimes minimum turnover or institutional affiliation. Individuals generally cannot apply.
asia_latam.realistic: Not usable as a policy-influence route by an ordinary person. This is a delivery body, not a deliberative one. It consults industry and academia through invited roundtables. An individual's realistic option is to apply to a funding call if eligible, or to raise IndiaAI issues through the MeitY consultation route or the Standing Committee instead.
asia_latam.note: CEO appointment VERIFIED via ANI, 5 June 2026. The DIC/IBD corporate structure is VERIFIED from MeitY recruitment advertisements issued under 'India AI Division, Digital India Corporation'. I did not find a published board or governing-council membership list — treat the internal governance above the CEO/COO level as UNVERIFIED.

asia_latam.body: AI Governance and Economic Group (AIGEG)
asia_latam.local_name: एआई गवर्नेंस एंड इकोनॉमिक ग्रुप
asia_latam.ai_jurisdiction: India's central institutional mechanism for AI governance policy development and inter-ministerial coordination. Mandate covers cross-sectoral AI governance, policy alignment across government, and labour-market impacts of AI. This is the seat where an Indian AI law would be shaped before it reaches Cabinet.

chair.name: Ashwini Vaishnaw
chair.role: Chairperson (Minister of Electronics and IT, Railways, and I&B). Vice-Chairperson: Jitin Prasada, Minister of State for Electronics & IT and Commerce & Industry.

asia_latam.current_business: Constituted 16 April 2026. Composed of senior Government of India stakeholders across policy development, science and technology, security and economic affairs. Supported by a Technology and Policy Expert Committee (TPEC) which advises it on global developments, emerging technologies, risks and regulation. Operationalises the India AI Governance Guidelines.
asia_latam.public_route: None. There is no public submission mechanism, no published meeting calendar, no minutes. Indirect routes only: a MeitY consultation, the Parliamentary Standing Committee, or an RTI application to MeitY for AIGEG records.
asia_latam.language: English.
asia_latam.threshold: RTI application fee INR 10. RTI is restricted to Indian citizens — foreign nationals cannot file.
asia_latam.realistic: Not usable directly. This is a closed inter-ministerial body of serving officials. Be honest with anyone planning engagement: the only handle an outsider has is RTI (citizens only) or influencing MeitY upstream. Membership of the TPEC is by invitation and the criteria are not published.
asia_latam.note: Chair, vice-chair, constitution date and the TPEC relationship VERIFIED from PIB Press Release PRID 2252739. Full membership list is stated in the release to be in a linked annex PDF which I did not retrieve — individual members beyond the chair and vice-chair are UNVERIFIED.

asia_latam.body: India AI Impact Summit 2026
asia_latam.local_name: भारत एआई इम्पैक्ट शिखर सम्मेलन 2026
asia_latam.ai_jurisdiction: Host of the fourth in the series of global AI summits (after Bletchley, Seoul, Paris). Held 19-20 February 2026 at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi. Organised by MeitY/IndiaAI under a 'Sutras and Chakras' framework. Set the agenda for Global South AI positioning; the India AI Governance Guidelines were foregrounded there.

chair.name: Ashwini Vaishnaw
chair.role: Minister responsible (MeitY); hosted by Prime Minister Narendra Modi

asia_latam.current_business: Concluded 20 February 2026. Current business is implementation and follow-through of summit outcomes. The Summit ran a formal pre-summit stakeholder consultation in June 2025 with dedicated category sessions for international organisations, industry, startups, academia AND civil society, plus a Global South Showcase and a research symposium. UN ODET ran side events.
asia_latam.public_route: The stakeholder consultation form at impact.indiaai.gov.in/stakeholder-consultation (now closed — the sessions it served ran in June 2025). Civil society was a named, separately-slotted category, so engagement was formally possible. Physical attendance required accreditation/registration. Side events were the more open route.
asia_latam.language: English.
asia_latam.threshold: No signature threshold. Accreditation and invitation controlled participation in the main programme.
asia_latam.realistic: Civil society engagement was real but curated. The stakeholder consultation genuinely had a civil-society slot, which is better than the Paris or Bletchley precedent. However, the window was in June 2025 — eight months before the event — so anyone who discovered the Summit in 2026 had already missed the substantive input point. The realistic lesson for future summits: the consultation opens roughly 6-9 months before, on the summit's own domain, not on the ministry's. Watch impact.indiaai.gov.in, not meity.gov.in.
asia_latam.note: Summit dates, venue and the existence of a civil-society consultation track VERIFIED from impact.indiaai.gov.in. The consultation sessions are dated June 2025 on that page; the page does not state whether the form remains open, and it appears to be historical.

asia_latam.body: MyGov (Citizen Engagement Platform)
asia_latam.local_name: माईगव
asia_latam.ai_jurisdiction: Cross-government citizen consultation platform under MeitY/Digital India Corporation. Used inconsistently for MeitY drafts; hosts discussions, polls, and 'Share your ideas' consultations, including on AI and digital policy.

chair.name: UNVERIFIED
chair.role: CEO, MyGov — I did not verify the current officeholder and am not naming one.

asia_latam.current_business: Runs alongside, not instead of, MeitY's email-based consultations. Not every MeitY AI consultation is mirrored here — the 2026 IT Rules AI-labelling consultation ran by email only.
asia_latam.public_route: Register a free account (mobile number or email), then comment on an open 'Discuss' or 'Consultation' task. Comments are public and visible to other users, which is the opposite of MeitY's confidential email route.
asia_latam.language: English and Hindi interface; some content in other Indian languages. No foreign-language support.
asia_latam.threshold: None. Free registration. Requires an Indian mobile number for some functions.
asia_latam.realistic: Usable and low-friction if a relevant consultation is live, and it is the only Indian route where your submission is publicly visible. But it is not the authoritative channel — for AI policy specifically, the email consultation is where MeitY actually reads submissions. Treat MyGov as supplementary. Do not rely on it as the only place you check for open windows.
asia_latam.note: Platform existence and function VERIFIED; I deliberately did not verify current MyGov leadership and have marked it UNVERIFIED rather than guess. MyGov's role relative to MeitY email consultations is inferred from the observed pattern that the April 2026 IT Rules consultation used email only.

asia_latam.body: House of Representatives Committee on Cabinet
asia_latam.local_name: 衆議院 内閣委員会
asia_latam.ai_jurisdiction: The lead Diet committee for AI. Handles legislation under the Cabinet Office, which owns the AI Act (人工知能関連技術の研究開発及び活用の推進に関する法律), the AI Strategy Headquarters, science and technology policy, digital policy and personal information protection. Japan's AI Act was scrutinised here.

chair.name: UNVERIFIED — see note
chair.role: 委員長 (Chair). The official roster dated 24 April 2026 lists YAMASHITA Takashi (山下貴司, LDP), but Yamashita became Minister of Justice in the cabinet inaugurated 17 September 2026 and cannot simultaneously chair the committee.

asia_latam.current_business: Implementation oversight of the AI Act (in force since 2025) and the AI Basic Plan Phase II adopted by Cabinet decision on 14 July 2026. The AI Act is a promotion statute with no penalties, so committee scrutiny is about plan implementation and budget rather than enforcement.
asia_latam.public_route: There is effectively no direct public-submission route to a Japanese Diet committee. Committees hear 参考人 (sankōnin, expert witnesses) and hold 公聴会 (kōchōkai, public hearings) on major bills, but witnesses are selected by the committee's 理事会 (board of directors) on party nomination. The Diet petition system (請願) requires a sitting Diet member to formally introduce your petition — you cannot file one yourself.
asia_latam.language: Japanese only. Proceedings, rosters and all submission procedures are Japanese-language. No English service.
asia_latam.threshold: No signature threshold, but the Diet petition route has a hard procedural gate: a Diet member must sponsor and introduce the petition (紹介議員). Without a sponsoring member it does not exist.
asia_latam.realistic: Not realistically usable by an outsider, and not usable at all by a non-Japanese speaker acting alone. Be blunt about this: the Japanese Diet has no equivalent of a select-committee call for written evidence. The practical route into Japanese AI policy is the executive branch's public comment system (e-Gov), not the legislature. If you must reach the committee, the realistic path is through a member's office or an affiliated industry/academic association.
asia_latam.note: The committee's existence, jurisdiction and membership URL are VERIFIED. The CHAIR IS NOT VERIFIED as of today: the live Shugiin roster page was still showing an as-of date of 24 April 2026 with Yamashita Takashi as chair, which is stale given the 17 September 2026 cabinet. Re-check the roster page directly — it carries a 現在 (as-of) date in the top-right which is the field to read. Do not cite Yamashita as current chair.

asia_latam.body: House of Councillors Committee on Cabinet
asia_latam.local_name: 参議院 内閣委員会
asia_latam.ai_jurisdiction: Upper-house counterpart. Same jurisdiction: Cabinet Office bills including AI, science and technology policy, digital, personal information protection. Reviews AI legislation after Lower House passage.

chair.name: KITAMURA Tsuneo (北村経夫)
chair.role: 委員長 (Chair), Liberal Democratic Party

asia_latam.current_business: AI Act implementation oversight and the AI Basic Plan Phase II. Committee composition: chair plus 4 理事 (directors) and 18 members, spanning LDP, CDP, DPP, Komeito, Ishin, Sanseitō, JCP and others.
asia_latam.public_route: Same as the Lower House: 参考人 (expert witness) appearance by committee invitation only, or a 請願 (petition) which requires a sitting Councillor to introduce it. No open written-evidence process.
asia_latam.language: Japanese only. The Sangiin site has a thin English section but committee rosters and petition procedure are Japanese-only.
asia_latam.threshold: Petition requires a sponsoring member (紹介議員). No numeric threshold.
asia_latam.realistic: Not realistically usable by an outsider. Same assessment as the Lower House committee. Its one practical advantage is that the Sangiin roster page is better maintained — it carried an as-of date of 21 September 2026, one day before this research, which is why this chair is verified and the Lower House one is not.
asia_latam.note: Chair VERIFIED from the official Sangiin roster page, as-of date 21 September 2026. Session context: the 221st Diet (special session) shown as running 18 February to 25 July 2026.

asia_latam.body: House of Representatives Committee on Economy, Trade and Industry
asia_latam.local_name: 衆議院 経済産業委員会
asia_latam.ai_jurisdiction: Scrutinises METI, which owns AI industrial policy, the AI Guidelines for Business (jointly with MIC), semiconductor and compute policy, and — new in 2026 — a dedicated AI Industry Strategy Division (AI産業戦略課). This is the committee for the industrial/economic side of AI rather than the governance framework side.

chair.name: KUDŌ Shōzō (工藤彰三)
chair.role: 委員長 (Chair)

asia_latam.current_business: METI oversight including the AI Industry Strategy Division established in 2026 and METI's role in delivering the AI Basic Plan Phase II. METI minister: AKAZAWA Ryosei.
asia_latam.public_route: 参考人 by invitation; 請願 requires a sponsoring member. No open call for written evidence. The productive route to METI policy is METI's own public comment channel, which feeds into e-Gov.
asia_latam.language: Japanese only.
asia_latam.threshold: Petition requires a sponsoring Diet member.
asia_latam.realistic: Not usable directly. Go to METI's consultation page instead — that is where an outsider's written input can actually land. Note that meti.go.jp/feedback renders poorly for automated fetching; the reliable aggregator is the e-Gov public comment portal.

asia_latam.local_name: 参議院 経済産業委員会
asia_latam.ai_jurisdiction: Upper-house METI oversight: AI industrial policy, compute and semiconductor strategy, AI Guidelines for Business.

chair.role: 委員長 (Chair)

asia_latam.language: Japanese only.
