asia_latam.body: Artificial Intelligence Strategy Headquarters
asia_latam.local_name: 人工知能戦略本部
asia_latam.ai_jurisdiction: The statutory apex AI body, established under the AI Act (人工知能関連技術の研究開発及び活用の推進に関する法律). Drafts and administers the AI Basic Plan (人工知能基本計画), coordinates all ministries on AI, and is the control tower for Japanese AI policy. Because it is statutory rather than advisory, it displaced the earlier non-statutory AI Strategy Council.

chair.name: TAKAICHI Sanae (高市早苗)
chair.role: 本部長 (Director-General) — ex officio as Prime Minister. Deputy Directors: KIHARA Minoru (Chief Cabinet Secretary) and the Minister of State for AI Strategy. Members: all other Ministers of State.

asia_latam.current_business: Adopted the first AI Basic Plan (人工知能基本計画, 'Trustworthy AI / Japan's Revival') by Cabinet decision on 23 December 2025. Adopted the AI Basic Plan Phase II (第Ⅱ期, 'Japan AX — stronger, richer') by Cabinet decision on 14 July 2026. A public comment on the Phase II draft (素案) opened 19 June 2026. Secretariat sits in the Cabinet Office.
asia_latam.public_route: The Headquarters itself does not take direct submissions. It exposes itself to the public exclusively through the e-Gov public comment system when it puts a draft Basic Plan or implementing order out — that is the single, real handle. Meeting agendas, distributed materials and summary minutes (議事要旨) are published on the Cabinet Office page after each meeting, which makes it unusually transparent to read even though it is closed to input.
asia_latam.language: Japanese only for the Headquarters pages and for e-Gov submissions.
asia_latam.threshold: None. Comment periods are, as a matter of the Administrative Procedure Act, in principle 30 days or more from the notice date.
asia_latam.realistic: Read-only for most people, but genuinely open at the plan-drafting moments. The 19 June 2026 Phase II draft consultation is the pattern to watch: when a Basic Plan is revised, a real 30-day window opens on e-Gov and anyone may submit. Outside those windows there is nothing to engage with. Note the Cabinet Office explicitly states it weighs comments on substance, not volume, so organised mass-identical submissions are discounted by design.
asia_latam.note: Structure, leadership formula, statutory basis and both Basic Plan cabinet decision dates VERIFIED from the Cabinet Office pages www8.cao.go.jp/cstp/ai/ai_hq/ai_hq.html and www8.cao.go.jp/cstp/ai/index.html. The Minister of State for AI Strategy as at the 17 September 2026 reshuffle is FURUKAWA Toshiharu (see separate entry); the Cabinet Office HQ page was still naming the previous holder, ONODA Kimi, indicating the page lags the reshuffle.

asia_latam.body: Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence Strategy / Minister for Digital Transformation
asia_latam.local_name: AI戦略担当大臣 / デジタル大臣
asia_latam.ai_jurisdiction: The named political owner of the AI brief. Concurrently Minister for Digital Transformation and Minister of State for Science and Technology Policy, plus cybersecurity, intellectual property, space and ocean policy. Deputy Director of the AI Strategy Headquarters.

chair.name: FURUKAWA Toshiharu
chair.role: Minister for Digital Transformation / Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence Strategy / Minister of State for Science and Technology Policy (plus further portfolios). Appointed in the Takaichi reshuffled cabinet inaugurated 17 September 2026. Predecessor in the AI Strategy brief: ONODA Kimi, who moved to Economic Security.

asia_latam.current_business: Delivering the AI Basic Plan Phase II (Cabinet decision 14 July 2026). Note the significant 2026 consolidation: AI Strategy, Digital Transformation and Science & Technology Policy are now held by one person, where in the first Takaichi cabinet (Oct 2025) AI Strategy sat with Science & Technology under Onoda and Digital sat separately.
asia_latam.public_route: No direct route to the minister. Digital Agency and Cabinet Office rule-making under this portfolio goes out for public comment via e-Gov.
asia_latam.language: The Kantei site has a full English mirror at japan.kantei.go.jp, which is genuinely useful and one of the few English-language Japanese government resources that is kept current. Consultation itself is Japanese-only.
asia_latam.threshold: None.
asia_latam.realistic: The minister is not directly reachable, but japan.kantei.go.jp is the correct authoritative English source for who holds the AI brief, and it is updated promptly — it already reflected the 17 September 2026 reshuffle. Use it rather than Wikipedia, which was still showing the October 2025 line-up.

Other ministers verified on the same page: AKAZAWA Ryosei (METI), FUJII Hisayuki (MIC), KIHARA Minoru (Chief Cabinet Secretary). asia_latam.body: AI Strategy Council
asia_latam.local_name: AI戦略会議
asia_latam.ai_jurisdiction: The non-statutory expert advisory council established in 2023 that produced Japan's interim AI policy positions and laid the groundwork for the AI Act. Now largely superseded.

chair.name: UNVERIFIED
chair.role: Chair — I did not verify the current or final chair and will not name one.

asia_latam.current_business: Largely dormant. The most recent meeting recorded on the Cabinet Office page is the 14th session on 2 June 2025, with the previous one on 4 February 2025. Its function has been absorbed by the statutory AI Strategy Headquarters and its expert panel (専門調査会). Included here specifically so it is not mistaken for the live body — a lot of secondary commentary still points at it.
asia_latam.public_route: None. Advisory body, closed membership. Agendas, distributed materials and summary minutes are published as PDFs after each meeting.
asia_latam.language: Japanese only.
asia_latam.threshold: None.
asia_latam.realistic: Not usable and, more importantly, no longer the right target. If someone directs you to the AI戦略会議 as Japan's AI control tower, that advice is out of date — go to the 人工知能戦略本部 instead.
asia_latam.note: Meeting history (last recorded session 2 June 2025) VERIFIED from the Cabinet Office page. The chair is deliberately left UNVERIFIED. The supersession by the statutory Headquarters is an inference from the meeting record plus the AI Act's creation of the Headquarters — stated here as an inference, not a fact.

asia_latam.body: e-Gov Public Comment (Administrative Procedure Act public comment procedure)
asia_latam.local_name: e-Gov パブリックコメント（意見公募手続）
asia_latam.ai_jurisdiction: The single mandatory consultation channel for all Japanese ministries when making 命令等 (cabinet orders, ministerial ordinances, notices/告示, administrative guidance). Every AI-related ordinance, notice and Basic Plan draft from the Cabinet Office, METI, MIC and the Digital Agency passes through here. Statutory basis: Administrative Procedure Act (行政手続法), Chapter 6. Policy oversight sits with MIC's Administrative Management Bureau.

chair.name: Not applicable
chair.role: System, not a body. Administered across government; procedure overseen by the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications (総務省行政管理局).

asia_latam.current_business: Continuously open. Live cases are listed on the portal's 意見募集中案件一覧. AI-relevant recent case: the AI Basic Plan Phase II draft (人工知能基本計画（素案）), comment call announced 19 June 2026.
asia_latam.public_route: Find the case on the portal, open it, read the 意見募集要項 (the case-specific comment call sheet — this is the load-bearing document), then use the 意見提出 (submit opinion) form. Required fields vary BY CASE and are controlled by that sheet: if a name/address/phone/email field is not displayed on the form, that information is not required. The only universally mandatory field is the opinion text itself, which has a character limit that will hard-error if exceeded. No account registration is required.
asia_latam.language: Japanese only. There is no English interface, no English guidance, and comments are expected in Japanese. Nothing formally bars a non-Japanese speaker or a foreign national from submitting — there is no nationality check — but in practice a submission that officials cannot read will not be processed meaningfully.
asia_latam.threshold: No signature or supporter threshold. Statutory minimum comment period: in principle 30 days or more from the notice date. The agency must publish a summary of comments received and its response when it finalises the rule.
asia_latam.realistic: This is the single most usable formal route in Japan and the one to actually recommend — no account, no fee, no nationality bar, a statutory 30-day floor, and a legal duty on the agency to publish its response to comments. Two honest limits. First, language: it is Japanese-only end to end, so a non-speaker needs a translated submission and cannot navigate the portal unaided; machine translation of the interface works but machine-translating your own submission into Japanese produces text officials visibly discount. Second, the system explicitly weights substance over volume and says identical repeated opinions do not get proportional weight — a coordinated campaign of identical comments is designed not to work here. One well-argued Japanese-language submission beats a thousand copies.
asia_latam.note: System description, the 30-day statutory floor, the no-account/conditional-fields submission mechanics and the substance-over-volume rule are all VERIFIED from the official e-Gov pages public-comment.e-gov.go.jp/contents/about-public-comment and /contents/help/guide/submission.html. The absence of English support is a verified negative — the official pages carry no language options and no guidance for foreign submitters. The e-Gov top page is JavaScript-rendered and will not load for simple fetchers; the /contents/ subpages do.

asia_latam.body: National Assembly Science, ICT, Broadcasting and Communications Committee
asia_latam.local_name: 국회 과학기술정보방송통신위원회 (과방위)
asia_latam.ai_jurisdiction: The lead standing committee for AI. Oversees the Ministry of Science and ICT (과학기술정보통신부), the Korea Communications Commission (방송통신위원회) and the Nuclear Safety and Security Commission (원자력안전위원회). It produced and passed the AI Framework Act (consolidating 19 separate bills) and handles all amendments to it, plus semiconductors, R&D budget and broadcasting.

chair.name: SONG Gi-heon (송기헌)
chair.role: 위원장 (Chair), Democratic Party of Korea, three-term member. Elected for the second half of the 22nd National Assembly.

asia_latam.current_business: Song took the chair on 30 June 2026, naming AI, semiconductors and broadcasting fairness as his stated priorities. Oversight of AI Framework Act implementation since its 22 January 2026 entry into force, and of MSIT's enforcement decree and notices. Note the political context: the People Power Party members reportedly submitted en-bloc resignation letters around the handover, so committee composition may be unstable.
asia_latam.public_route: Two routes. (1) 입법예고 (legislative pre-announcement) on National Assembly bills — bills referred to committee are posted for public comment on the Assembly's bill information system, typically 10 days, and anyone may submit written opinions online. (2) 공청회 (public hearings) with invited witnesses, by committee selection. The separate 국민동의청원 petition route (below) also lands bills in this committee.
asia_latam.language: Korean only. The committee site (science.na.go.kr) and the bill pre-announcement system are Korean-language. The National Assembly has an English site but it does not carry participation functions.
asia_latam.threshold: No threshold for a written 입법예고 opinion. Requires the standard Korean identity verification for the Assembly's online systems.
asia_latam.realistic: The 입법예고 route is formally open and genuinely used, but it has two practical gates that exclude most outsiders: everything is in Korean, and the Assembly's online systems generally require Korean identity verification (본인인증) which in practice needs a Korean mobile number or a joint certificate — foreign residents with an ARC can often do this, foreign non-residents usually cannot. The 10-day window is also short. For a non-Korean-speaker this is effectively closed without a Korean intermediary.
asia_latam.note: Chair and date VERIFIED via Korean press reporting of the 30 June 2026 Democratic Party decision and vote (Song selected over Lee Eon-ju). Jurisdiction over MSIT/KCC/NSSC VERIFIED from Korean Wikipedia. The official committee site science.na.go.kr blocks automated access via robots.txt, so the member list was not directly retrieved — individual member names are UNVERIFIED. The site is served on port 444 in some links (science.na.go.kr:444); the standard URL above should resolve for a human browser.

asia_latam.body: Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT)
asia_latam.local_name: 과학기술정보통신부 (과기정통부)
asia_latam.ai_jurisdiction: The competent authority under the AI Framework Act. Powers include: investigating suspected violations and conducting on-site inspections (Art. 40), issuing corrective orders and service suspension orders, confirming on request whether a system is 'high-impact AI', and drafting the Presidential Decree and notices. Also owns national AI R&D, compute and the AI Safety Institute.

chair.name: BAE Kyung-hoon (배경훈)
chair.role: Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Science and ICT (부총리 겸 과학기술정보통신부 장관)

asia_latam.current_business: Implementing the AI Framework Act, in force 22 January 2026. Released the draft regulatory package for public comment on 8 September 2025: Enforcement Decree, Safety Assurance Notice (using a 10^26 FLOP training-compute threshold plus risk criteria), Business Responsibilities Notice for high-impact AI operators, AI Safety Guidelines, and the High-Impact AI Determination Guideline. MSIT has indicated a one-year grace period before administrative fines are imposed — i.e. to roughly January 2027. The minister's elevation to Deputy Prime Minister rank is itself significant: AI policy now sits at DPM level.
asia_latam.public_route: Ministry rule-making goes through 입법예고 / 행정예고 (legislative and administrative pre-announcement) posted on the Government Legislation Centre's citizen participation portal, 국민참여입법센터. Anyone may submit an opinion online against a specific posted draft. MSIT also runs 공청회 (public hearings) and 간담회 (roundtables) on major AI notices, generally invitation-based.
asia_latam.language: Korean only. 국민참여입법센터 has no English interface and drafts are published only in Korean.
asia_latam.threshold: No threshold. Statutory pre-announcement periods: normally 40 days for 입법예고 of decrees, 20 days for 행정예고 of notices — shorter in urgent cases, which MSIT has used.
asia_latam.realistic: Formally open to anyone including foreign companies and individuals — Korea does not restrict pre-announcement comments by nationality, and international law firms routinely file on behalf of clients. But it is Korean-language end to end and the portal's submission function generally expects Korean identity verification. The honest assessment: usable by a Korean speaker or through Korean counsel; not usable unaided by a non-speaker. The 10^26 FLOP threshold and the high-impact criteria were both meaningfully shaped by comments in the 2025 window, so this route does have demonstrated influence.
asia_latam.note: Minister VERIFIED same-day (22 September 2026) from Korean press coverage of him speaking as 부총리 겸 과학기술정보통신부 장관. Act effective date (22 Jan 2026), the September 2025 regulatory package contents, the 10^26 FLOP threshold and the one-year fine grace period VERIFIED from Baker Botts and Cooley analyses. I could not verify whether the enforcement decree has since been finalised in its consulted form — treat the final text as UNVERIFIED.

asia_latam.body: National AI Committee
asia_latam.local_name: 국가인공지능위원회 (National AI Strategy Committee / 국가인공지능전략위원회 — naming UNVERIFIED, see note)
asia_latam.ai_jurisdiction: Presidentially-chaired apex AI body referenced in the AI Framework Act. Article 34 empowers it to impose additional safety and reliability requirements on high-impact AI deployers beyond the Act's baseline — a genuinely substantive power, not merely advisory. Functions as the national AI control tower above MSIT.

chair.name: UNVERIFIED
chair.role: Chaired ex officio by the President of the Republic of Korea (currently Lee Jae-myung). The vice-chair and the private-sector membership were not verified and are not named here.

asia_latam.current_business: Operative under the AI Framework Act since 22 January 2026. Its Article 34 power to add requirements on high-impact AI is the provision to watch, because it lets Korea tighten obligations without amending the statute.
asia_latam.public_route: No direct public submission route. Indirect only: comment on MSIT drafts via 국민참여입법센터, or reach the committee's agenda through the National Assembly's 과방위.
asia_latam.language: Korean only.
asia_latam.threshold: None applicable.
asia_latam.realistic: Not usable directly. A presidentially-chaired committee with closed membership. Its importance to an outside observer is analytical rather than participatory: because Article 34 lets it add binding requirements administratively, watching its output matters more than trying to address it.
asia_latam.note: MARKED UNVERIFIED ON NAME AND MEMBERSHIP. The Act's creation of a presidentially-chaired national AI committee and its Article 34 power are VERIFIED from FPF and Cooley analyses of the Act, which use the English rendering 'National AI Committee'. Separately, Korean-language sources use 국가인공지능전략위원회 ('National AI Strategy Committee') for a body launched under the Lee administration. I could not establish within this research whether these are the same body, a renaming, or two distinct structures. Resolve this before citing — do not treat the Korean and English names above as confirmed equivalents, and do not name a vice-chair.

asia_latam.body: AI Safety Institute (Korea AISI)
asia_latam.local_name: AI안전연구소
asia_latam.ai_jurisdiction: Statutory body established under the AI Framework Act to evaluate AI risk and develop safety standards. Korea's node in the International Network of AI Safety Institutes. Co-produced the bilingual Korea AI Basic Act resource with the Future of Life Institute.

chair.name: KIM Myuhngjoo
chair.role: Director, AI Safety Institute

asia_latam.current_business: Operates under MSIT with the Electronics and Telecommunications Research Institute (ETRI) as host/supporting organisation — note this dual line: it is statutorily grounded but institutionally embedded in a government research institute rather than standing alone. Work programme covers AI safety policy, evaluation methodology and international AISI collaboration.
asia_latam.public_route: No formal comment mechanism. Practical routes: research collaboration enquiries and general contact via aisi.re.kr; international engagement through the AI Safety Institute network; policy input indirectly via MSIT pre-announcement.
asia_latam.language: Korean and English. Korea AISI maintains a genuine English site — a notable exception in this jurisdiction and the most accessible Korean AI body for a non-Korean speaker.
asia_latam.threshold: None; no formal participation process exists to have a threshold.
asia_latam.realistic: Not a participation route in any formal sense, but it is the most approachable Korean AI institution for an outsider because it has a working English presence and an internationally-facing research remit. Researchers and technical contributors can realistically make contact. Ordinary citizens have no route here and should use the petition or the MSIT pre-announcement instead.
asia_latam.note: Director and the MSIT/ETRI institutional relationship VERIFIED from the institute's own English site aisi.re.kr/eng/contents/23 and its site footer. The statutory basis under the AI Framework Act is VERIFIED indirectly via Cooley's analysis, which refers to an 'AI Safety Research Institute' established by the law; the exact article number is UNVERIFIED.

asia_latam.body: National Assembly National Petition System (electronic petition with public assent)
asia_latam.local_name: 국민동의청원 (국회전자청원)
asia_latam.ai_jurisdiction: Not AI-specific, but AI petitions are routed to the 과학기술정보방송통신위원회. This is the one route in this entire research with a genuine, automatic legislative trigger, which is why it deserves precise treatment.

chair.name: Not applicable
chair.role: System operated by the National Assembly Secretariat.

asia_latam.current_business: Continuously open. Any petition reaching threshold is referred to the subject-matter standing committee.
asia_latam.public_route: Precise mechanism, in three stages. (1) REGISTRATION: an identity-verified citizen drafts a petition. (2) PUBLICITY GATE: the petition must gather 100 supporters within a set window; the Assembly then conducts a compliance/legality review within 7 days, and if it passes, the petition becomes publicly listed. (3) ASSENT: 50,000 signatures within 30 days of public listing. On reaching 50,000 the petition is 성립 (established) and is AUTOMATICALLY REFERRED to the relevant standing committee, which is then obliged to take it up as a formal agenda item under its petition-review procedure. The threshold was lowered from 100,000 to 50,000 in December 2021. Both petitioning and signing require real-name authentication (본인인증), which eliminates duplicate-account inflation — a deliberate design difference from the former Blue House petition system.
asia_latam.language: Korean only. No English interface. Identity verification is built on Korean domestic authentication infrastructure.
asia_latam.threshold: 100 supporters to pass the publicity gate; then 50,000 verified signatures within 30 days to be formally established and referred to committee. Real-name authentication required to create or to sign.
asia_latam.realistic: The trigger is real and this is the most powerful citizen route in any of the four jurisdictions covered — 50,000 verified signatures compel committee referral, which no other system here does. But be honest about two things. First, referral is not action: Korean press and civic groups have documented petitions that cleared 50,000 and were then left without a single 청원심사소위 review session, sometimes indefinitely, with the criticism '5만명 동의 받으면 뭐하나' ('what good is 50,000 signatures'). The trigger compels referral, not consideration, and certainly not legislation. Second, the real-name authentication gate means it is a Korean-citizens-and-residents system in practice; a non-Korean-speaker cannot use it and a non-resident generally cannot authenticate. Within those limits, an ordinary Korean citizen genuinely can use it, and 50,000 in 30 days is achievable for a motivated constituency.
asia_latam.note: The two-stage threshold (100 then 50,000/30 days), the December 2021 reduction from 100,000, the automatic committee referral and the real-name authentication requirement are VERIFIED from Korean-language sources including the National Assembly's own guidance page (assembly.go.kr menuNo=600249, which blocks automated fetching via robots.txt but is publicly readable). The portal URL is VERIFIED as the National Assembly e-petition site (국회전자청원). The post-referral inaction problem is VERIFIED from Korean press criticism (Newstomato, Danbi News).

asia_latam.body: Special Committee on Artificial Intelligence (on PL 2338/2023)
asia_latam.local_name: Comissão Especial sobre Inteligência Artificial (PL 2338/23) — Câmara dos Deputados
asia_latam.ai_jurisdiction: The decisive seat for Brazilian AI regulation right now. A temporary special committee of the Chamber of Deputies, 57th Legislature, created to analyse PL 2338/2023 (the Marco Legal da IA) after the Senate passed it. Under Brazil's rapporteur system, the relator's substitutive text is what the Chamber votes on — the relator, not the committee president, is the controlling seat.

chair.name: Luisa Canziani (President) and Aguinaldo Ribeiro (Relator)
chair.role: Presidente: Dep. Luisa Canziani (PSD-PR). Relator: Dep. Aguinaldo Ribeiro (PP-PB), designated 20 May 2025. Committee installed 20 May 2025. Secretary-Executive: Ana Karina de Macedo Tito, +55 61 3216-6235.

asia_latam.current_business: Status as of September 2026: 'Aguardando Parecer do(a) Relator(a) na Comissão Especial' — still awaiting the rapporteur's opinion, sixteen months after his designation. 31 meetings held, 180 guests heard, 163 proposals voted. 37 bills now appended (apensados) to PL 2338/2023, with further appendings approved by the Mesa Diretora on 17 June, 1 September and 2 September 2026. The bill is under regime de prioridade (Art. 151, II, RICD) and will go to Plenary. The government's own AI governance bill creating the Sistema Nacional de Governança para a IA (SIA), proposed December 2025, was articulated with the relator and folded into this process. Separately PL 762/2026 (Rubens Pereira Júnior, PT-MA, 25 Feb 2026, high-consequence-sector AI framework amending the LGPD, Marco Civil and Consumer Code) was appended to PL 7132/2025 and received by this committee on 6 April 2026.
asia_latam.public_route: Three real routes. (1) AUDIÊNCIAS PÚBLICAS — the committee has held 31 meetings and heard 180 guests; hearing requests are made by deputies, but civil society organisations are routinely invited and Data Privacy Brasil, IDEC and others have appeared. The route for an outsider is to ask a committee member to request your inclusion. (2) Written contributions sent directly to the committee secretariat or to the relator's office (gabinete) — Brazilian practice accepts and often publishes these as 'contribuições'. (3) e-Democracia, the Chamber's citizen participation portal, which runs Wikilegis text-commenting and enquetes on bills.
asia_latam.language: Portuguese only. The Chamber portal has no functional English participation layer.
asia_latam.threshold: No threshold for written contributions or e-Democracia comments. Speaking at a hearing requires a deputy's request (requerimento) approved by the committee.
asia_latam.realistic: Better than most. Brazil's legislature is genuinely more porous to civil society than Japan's or Korea's — 180 guests heard is a real number, and organised Brazilian civil society has demonstrably shaped this text. But 'ordinary person' is a stretch: hearing slots go to organisations, and the effective lever is the relator's office, which is lobbied intensively and privately. A Portuguese-speaking individual can file a written contribution and comment on e-Democracia at no cost and with no gatekeeping, and that is a real if modest channel. A non-Portuguese speaker is effectively excluded. Note also that the committee has been 'awaiting the relator's opinion' since 2025 — the schedule slips repeatedly, so windows that look closed often reopen.
asia_latam.note: President and relator VERIFIED from the Chamber's own news release (camara.leg.br/noticias/1160383, dated 20 May 2025) and the relator designation VERIFIED from the bill's tramitação sheet (idProposicao 2487262). Meeting/guest/proposal counts and current status VERIFIED from the committee's official page. The /membros sub-page returned HTTP 500 during this research, so the current full membership list is UNVERIFIED — the URL is given because it is the correct official location, not because it was read.

asia_latam.body: Federal Senate — Temporary Internal Commission on Artificial Intelligence (concluded) and Senate Plenary
asia_latam.local_name: Comissão Temporária Interna sobre Inteligência Artificial no Brasil (CTIA) — Senado Federal
asia_latam.ai_jurisdiction: Originating chamber for PL 2338/2023. The CTIA analysed the bill and produced the favourable opinion that the Senate plenary adopted. Its work is done; the Senate regains jurisdiction only if the Chamber amends the text, in which case it returns for a final Senate vote.

chair.name: Eduardo Gomes (Relator, concluded)
chair.role: Relator: Sen. Eduardo Gomes (PL-TO), who filed successive reports between June and December 2024. Author of PL 2338/2023: Sen. Rodrigo Pacheco (PSD-MG), presented 3 May 2023.

asia_latam.current_business: CONCLUDED IN THE SENATE. Approved by the Senate plenary on 10 December 2024 (Parecer nº 207/2024-PLEN/SF) and remitted to the Chamber of Deputies on 17 March 2025. Anyone targeting the Senate for AI regulation in 2026 is targeting the wrong chamber — the action is in the Chamber's special committee. The Senate's remaining role is the final revision vote if the Chamber changes the text, which it certainly will given 37 appended bills.
asia_latam.public_route: Senate e-Cidadania: 'Consulta Pública' allows any registered user to vote for or against, and comment on, any bill under consideration in the Senate; 'Audiências Interativas' allow live questions to hearing witnesses. Both remain available for any Senate matter.
asia_latam.language: Portuguese only.
asia_latam.threshold: None for consultation voting or commenting. Free registration required.
asia_latam.realistic: The Senate consultation tools are genuinely easy — free registration, click to support or oppose, leave a comment, no gatekeeping. But for AI specifically this is now a dead channel: the bill left the Senate in March 2025. Included here so the seat is correctly identified as historical rather than current. Re-engage with the Senate only when the Chamber returns an amended text.
asia_latam.note: Senate approval date (10 December 2024), the parecer number, the relator, the author and the 17 March 2025 remittance to the Chamber are all VERIFIED from the Senate's own matéria page for PL 2338/2023. CTIA membership is UNVERIFIED — the commission is dissolved and its roster was not retrieved.

asia_latam.body: Autoridade Nacional de Proteção de Dados (National Data Protection Authority)
asia_latam.local_name: Autoridade Nacional de Proteção de Dados (ANPD)
asia_latam.ai_jurisdiction: Currently: data protection enforcement under the LGPD where AI processes personal data, plus a Regulatory Sandbox for AI project. Prospectively: the leading candidate to coordinate the Sistema Nacional de Governança da IA (SIA). ANPD filed formal proposed amendments to the substitutive text of PL 2338 — it is an active participant in shaping its own future mandate, not a passive recipient.

chair.name: UNVERIFIED
chair.role: Director-President — I did not verify the current officeholder and will not name one. ANPD is governed by a five-member Conselho Diretor appointed by the President with Senate confirmation, plus a multi-stakeholder Conselho Nacional de Proteção de Dados (CNPD).

asia_latam.current_business: AI Regulatory Sandbox project (an international award finalist). Open 'tomadas de subsídios' (calls for contributions) for its regulatory agenda, with contributions accepted until 16 October, including a topic on 'IA e proteção dos dados dos Titulares' (AI and data subjects' data protection). Proposed amendments to the PL 2338 substitutive are published on its site. Competing 2026 bills (PL 762/2026, PL 704/2026) would give ANPD the lead AI supervisory role with mandatory algorithmic impact assessments.
asia_latam.public_route: Two formal instruments. (1) CONSULTA PÚBLICA — formal public consultation on a draft regulation, with a published response. (2) TOMADA DE SUBSÍDIOS — an earlier-stage, more open call for evidence used to shape the regulatory agenda before drafting. Both are announced on gov.br/anpd and usually run through the federal Participa + Brasil platform. There is also a complaints channel (petição de titular) for individual LGPD violations, which is a genuine individual remedy.
asia_latam.language: Portuguese only.
asia_latam.threshold: None. Open to any person or organisation. The individual complaint route requires first attempting contact with the controller.
asia_latam.realistic: Genuinely usable, and the tomada de subsídios instrument is unusually open — it invites input before a draft exists, which is the stage at which input actually matters. Any Portuguese speaker can file. The ANPD publishes contributions and its responses. The one honest caveat: the 16 October deadline mentioned on its site does not state a year on the page as read, so confirm the year before relying on it. The individual complaint channel is a real, working remedy for an ordinary person whose data was misused by an AI system — that is the most concretely useful thing in this entry.
asia_latam.note: ANPD's AI sandbox, its open tomadas de subsídios including an AI-and-data-protection topic, and its formal amendment proposals to PL 2338 are VERIFIED from gov.br/anpd. THE DIRECTOR-PRESIDENT IS DELIBERATELY UNVERIFIED AND UNNAMED — the site's leadership page was not retrieved and I will not guess. The 16 October deadline is verified as stated on the site but its year is UNVERIFIED. The claim that ANPD will lead the SIA is a proposal in pending bills, NOT current law.

asia_latam.body: Senate e-Cidadania — Ideia Legislativa
asia_latam.local_name: Portal e-Cidadania — Ideia Legislativa / Sugestão Legislativa
asia_latam.ai_jurisdiction: Not AI-specific. A general citizen-initiated legislative proposal channel with a real numeric trigger, usable for an AI proposal.

chair.name: Not applicable
chair.role: Operated by the Federal Senate. Successful ideas are handled by the Comissão de Direitos Humanos e Legislação Participativa (CDH).

asia_latam.current_business: Continuously open. Cumulative platform figures run to roughly 148,000 ideas submitted, 80,000 authors and 12.5 million supports, which tells you the base rate: the overwhelming majority never clear threshold. A first Sugestão Legislativa of 2026 reached the CDH in January 2026, and a military-pay proposal cleared 20,000 in mid-2026 — so the mechanism does fire, a few times a year.
asia_latam.public_route: Register free on the e-Cidadania portal. Submit an Ideia Legislativa (you may submit several, but not duplicates of your own open ones). It then has exactly 4 months to gather 20,000 supports from other registered users. On reaching 20,000 it is forwarded to the CDH and formalised as a Sugestão Legislativa (SUG), which senators debate in that committee; the CDH issues a final opinion, and a favourable one can become a Senate bill. Ideas that miss the threshold close after 4 months but remain permanently readable on the portal.
asia_latam.language: Portuguese only.
asia_latam.threshold: 20,000 supports within 4 months. Free registration required to submit and to support. The portal explicitly warns users not to post CPF, ID numbers, phone numbers or addresses in the idea text.
asia_latam.realistic: Formally strong, practically hard. Like Korea's system it has a genuine automatic trigger — 20,000 supports forces the idea onto the CDH's agenda as a Sugestão Legislativa. Unlike Korea's, the ceiling is lower: the CDH issues an opinion, and converting that into law still requires the ordinary legislative process. And 20,000 supports in 4 months requires real organised mobilisation; out of ~148,000 ideas submitted, successes are counted in the dozens, and the ones that succeed are typically backed by a large occupational constituency (e.g. military pay). An individual with no organisation behind them will not clear it. Registration and submission themselves are genuinely free and open to any Portuguese speaker.
asia_latam.note: The 20,000-in-4-months threshold, the CDH referral, the conversion to Sugestão Legislativa and the registration/duplication rules are VERIFIED from the Senate's own 'como funciona' page. Cumulative platform statistics VERIFIED from the Senate's published e-Cidadania report PDF. Note there is a pending proposal to revise the admission criteria for Ideias Legislativas — the rules above are current but under review.

asia_latam.body: Chamber of Deputies e-Democracia and Participa + Brasil
asia_latam.local_name: Portal e-Democracia (Câmara dos Deputados) / Participa + Brasil (Governo Federal)
asia_latam.ai_jurisdiction: Two general-purpose participation platforms covering AI when an AI bill or an AI-related regulation is open. e-Democracia covers Chamber bills including PL 2338/2023 and its 37 appended bills; Participa + Brasil covers executive-branch consultations including ANPD's.

chair.name: Not applicable
chair.role: e-Democracia operated by the Chamber of Deputies; Participa + Brasil operated by the federal executive (Controladoria-Geral da União / Secretaria-Geral da Presidência). Brasil Participativo is a related Decidim-based platform run by the Presidency.

asia_latam.current_business: e-Democracia offers Wikilegis (clause-by-clause commenting on bill text), enquetes (polls for/against a bill), and Audiências Interativas (submit questions live during committee hearings, which deputies read out). The Chamber has announced a restructuring of the e-Democracia portal, so URLs and feature names may shift. Participa + Brasil hosts open federal consultations with comment forms.
asia_latam.public_route: e-Democracia: free registration, then comment on a bill's text in Wikilegis, vote in an enquete, or submit a question during a live committee hearing. Participa + Brasil: open the consultation, fill the form; some consultations do not require registration.
asia_latam.language: Portuguese only on both platforms.
asia_latam.threshold: None on either. No signature or supporter counts. Free, and largely registration-light.
asia_latam.realistic: These are the genuinely low-friction Brazilian routes for an ordinary person and the ones to recommend first. Audiências Interativas in particular are a real and underused lever: you can put a question directly into a live committee hearing on PL 2338 and have a deputy read it aloud, at zero cost and with no gatekeeper. Honest limits: comments carry no obligation on anyone to respond, Wikilegis contributions are advisory, and reach depends on whether staff choose to compile them. Portuguese-only. But 'can an ordinary person actually use this' — yes, unambiguously, for a Brazilian.
asia_latam.note: Both platforms VERIFIED as live official portals. The announced restructuring of e-Democracia is VERIFIED from the Chamber's own notice page — expect URL churn. The specific feature set (Wikilegis, enquetes, audiências interativas) is drawn from official Chamber participation documentation; confirm current feature availability after the restructuring.

asia_latam.body: GENERIC METHOD — locating the AI policy seat and the public route in an arbitrary jurisdiction
asia_latam.local_name: n/a
asia_latam.ai_jurisdiction: Applies to any parliamentary or presidential system not covered above.

chair.name: Not applicable
chair.role: Method, not a body.

asia_latam.current_business:
STEP 1 — FIND THE COMMITTEE. Go to the parliament's official domain (almost always a .gov/.gob/.gouv/.parl/.leg national domain; find it via the Inter-Parliamentary Union's Parline database at data.ipu.org, which lists every national parliament with its official site). Look for the page named 'Committees' / 'Commissions' / 'Ausschüsse' / 'Comisiones' / '委員会' / '위원회'. AI almost never has its own standing committee. It sits in one of four places, and you should check in this order: (a) the committee shadowing the ICT/digital/communications ministry — the single most common home; (b) the committee shadowing science, technology, innovation or research; (c) the committee shadowing economy/industry/trade, where AI is framed as industrial policy; (d) the justice, home affairs or constitutional committee, where AI is framed as rights, surveillance or liability. In bicameral systems check both chambers — they often differ, and the upper house is frequently more accessible. Also search the site for 'special committee', 'select committee', 'ad hoc', 'temporary' or 'inquiry' plus 'artificial intelligence': many jurisdictions create a one-off AI committee that outranks the standing one, as Brazil and the EU did. CROSS-CHECK against the OECD.AI policy observatory (oecd.ai/en/dashboards) and the IPU's AI tracker, both of which index national AI bodies and are more current than Wikipedia.

STEP 2 — FIND THE CHAIR. The committee's own page on the parliament site carries the chair and member list; this is the only source to trust. Look for an 'as of' or 'current as at' date stamp on the roster — Japan and Korea both print one, and it is the field that tells you whether the page is stale. Two hard rules learned the hard way in this research. First, NEVER use Wikipedia for a current officeholder: English Wikipedia's Japanese cabinet article was eleven months out of date. Second, ALWAYS check whether the person you found has since been promoted into the executive — in parliamentary systems a committee chair who joins the cabinet must vacate the chair, and rosters lag by weeks. If a roster is stale, corroborate with a same-month news report naming the person in that role. If you cannot corroborate, say UNVERIFIED and give the live URL rather than naming a stale person.

STEP 3 — FIND WHETHER SUBMISSIONS ARE ACCEPTED. Search the committee or parliament site for: 'call for evidence', 'written submissions', 'inquiry', 'consultation', 'memorandum', 'contribución', 'contribuição', 'Stellungnahme', 'audition', '意見募集', '입법예고'. Three patterns exist and they determine everything. PATTERN A, OPEN CALL (Westminster-derived systems — UK, Canada, Australia, NZ, Ireland, India for Bills, South Africa): the committee publishes a call for written evidence with a deadline and an upload form or email; anyone worldwide may submit; submissions are usually published. This is the best case. PATTERN B, PRE-ANNOUNCEMENT (Korea, Japan, most civil-law systems): the legislature is closed, but the EXECUTIVE must publish draft rules for a statutory comment period; go there instead. PATTERN C, CLOSED (Japan's Diet, many others): witnesses by invitation only and petitions require a member's sponsorship; there is no direct route and you must work through a member's office or an affiliated association. Do not pretend Pattern C is Pattern A.

STEP 4 — THE FOUR UNIVERSAL ROUTES. In nearly every democracy exactly these four exist, in descending order of usefulness. (1) MINISTRY CONSULTATION / NOTICE-AND-COMMENT. Nearly always the highest-value route, because it is statutory, has a defined minimum period, and frequently obliges the agency to publish a response. Find it at the ministry's 'consultations' page or a central portal: e-Gov (Japan), 국민참여입법센터 (Korea), Participa+Brasil (Brazil), regulations.gov (US), 'Have your say' (EU), gov.uk/government/consultations (UK), consultations.gc.ca (Canada). Search '<country> public consultation portal' plus the local-language term. (2) COMMITTEE EVIDENCE. Highest visibility when Pattern A applies; your text may be published and cited. Zero cost. (3) PETITION. Check whether it has a real trigger or is symbolic — this is the single most important distinction and most people get it wrong. Real triggers: Korea 50,000/30 days forces committee referral; Brazil Senate 20,000/4 months forces CDH consideration; UK 100,000 forces a Westminster Hall debate; EU ECI 1 million across 7 states forces a Commission response; Germany Bundestag 50,000/4 weeks gets a public committee hearing. Symbolic: petitions requiring a legislator's sponsorship (Japan), or with no numeric consequence at all. Always establish what the number actually compels — in every case above it compels PROCESS, never an outcome, and Korea's experience shows referral can be followed by indefinite inaction. (4) OMBUDSMAN / DATA PROTECTION AUTHORITY / HUMAN RIGHTS INSTITUTION. Underrated and often the only route with a binding individual remedy. Where AI touches personal data, the DPA usually has jurisdiction TODAY under existing data protection law, without waiting for an AI act — and unlike a committee it must respond to a complaint. Find the DPA via the Global Privacy Assembly member list; find the ombudsman via the International Ombudsman Institute; find the national human rights institution via GANHRI. A fifth route worth knowing: FREEDOM OF INFORMATION. Roughly 130 countries have an access-to-information law; an FOI request is often the only way to see inside a closed inter-ministerial AI body. Check whether your country's law is open to foreigners — India's RTI is citizens-only, the EU's and the UK's are not.

STEP 5 — SANITY CHECKS BEFORE YOU ACT. Confirm the legislature is in session (committees do not meet in recess, and rosters are reconstituted at session start — India reconstitutes standing committees around September, so a chair verified in June may be wrong in October). Confirm the bill is in the chamber you think it is: Brazil's PL 2338 left the Senate in March 2025 and anyone still lobbying senators in 2026 is wasting effort. Confirm whether an AI-specific body has displaced the one you found: Japan's AI Strategy Council was superseded by the statutory AI Strategy Headquarters and most secondary commentary still points at the dead one. And confirm the language reality — if the route is single-language and requires domestic identity verification, as Korea's and to a lesser degree Japan's are, say so plainly rather than presenting a route the person cannot actually walk.
asia_latam.public_route: See STEP 4. In priority order: ministry notice-and-comment, committee written evidence, petition with a verified trigger, ombudsman/DPA complaint, FOI request.
asia_latam.language: Method is language-neutral. Applying it is not: assume the participation layer of any national system is monolingual in the national language even when the ministry maintains an English site, and budget for translation. English-language government pages are usually the PR layer, not the participation layer — the Kantei English site is a rare exception that is genuinely current.
asia_latam.threshold: Varies. The discipline is to always ask two questions of any threshold: what number, over what period — and then the question most people skip: what exactly does hitting it COMPEL? In every real-trigger system documented here, the answer is 'a procedural step', never a policy outcome.
asia_latam.realistic: This method is reliable for locating the seat and the route. It cannot make a closed system open. The honest headline finding across all four jurisdictions researched: the executive-branch consultation route is consistently more open, more predictable and more consequential than the legislative route, and it is the one to use by default. Legislative committees are more visible but far more gatekept. The second finding: language is the dominant practical barrier, not formal eligibility — Japan, Korea and Brazil all impose no nationality bar on written comments, yet all three are effectively closed to a non-speaker acting alone. Budget for a native-language submission or a local intermediary, or accept that the route is theoretical.
asia_latam.note: This is methodology, not a factual claim about any one body, so 'verified' refers to the method having been derived from and tested against the four jurisdictions researched above rather than asserted abstractly. The specific petition thresholds cited for Korea and Brazil are VERIFIED in their own entries above. The thresholds cited for the UK (100,000), EU ECI (1 million / 7 states) and Germany (50,000 / 4 weeks) are from background knowledge and were NOT verified in this research — treat them as UNVERIFIED starting points and confirm on the relevant official site before relying on them. data.ipu.org, oecd.ai and the IPU AI tracker are verified as live authoritative directories.
